  • Knowing the uncaught error categories prevents designing error handling that assumes TRY/CATCH will catch everything — avoiding silent failure scenarios
  • Always checking IF @@TRANCOUNT > 0 before ROLLBACK in CATCH handles the case where the error occurred before the BEGIN TRANSACTION — rolling back with zero active transactions would itself raise an error
  • Severity 20+ connection-terminating errors require connection-level handling in the C# application, not stored procedure TRY/CATCH

Fintech Example: A payment processing stored procedure with TRY/CATCH appeared to handle all errors correctly in testing. In production, occasional severity 22 (hardware error) events crashed the connection without the CATCH block executing — the payment was left in an inconsistent state. Adding idempotency keys and a recovery job that finds and resolves in-flight payment states addressed the class of errors that TRY/CATCH fundamentally cannot handle.

questions.tip: Template to memorise: BEGIN TRY → BEGIN TRANSACTION → DML → COMMIT → END TRY. BEGIN CATCH → IF @@TRANCOUNT>0 ROLLBACK → log error (ERROR_MESSAGE/LINE/PROCEDURE) → THROW (re-raise). Always check @@TRANCOUNT before ROLLBACK. Use THROW (not RAISERROR) for new SQL Server 2012+ code.

questions.question: How do you retrieve the identity value after an INSERT? Explain SCOPE_IDENTITY(), @@IDENTITY, and IDENT_CURRENT().
questions.answer:
Definition: SQL Server provides three ways to retrieve an auto-generated identity value after INSERT. SCOPE_IDENTITY() returns the last identity generated in the current scope and session — the safe, recommended choice. @@IDENTITY returns the last identity generated in the current session regardless of scope — unsafe when AFTER INSERT triggers insert into other identity tables. IDENT_CURRENT('table') returns the last identity for a specific table from any session — unsafe in concurrent environments.

Advantages:

  • SCOPE_IDENTITY() is immune to trigger interference — it only sees identity values generated in the current scope, not in trigger scopes
  • The OUTPUT clause captures all generated identity values for multi-row inserts — SCOPE_IDENTITY() only returns the last one from a multi-row INSERT
  • Using the correct function prevents silent identity mismatch bugs that only manifest in production when triggers are present

Fintech Example: A payment stored procedure inserted a Payment row and then used @@IDENTITY to get the PaymentId for inserting related PaymentLineItems. An AFTER INSERT trigger on Payments also inserted into an AuditLog table with its own identity column — @@IDENTITY returned the AuditLog's identity, not the Payment's. Switching to SCOPE_IDENTITY() returned the correct PaymentId, fixing the orphaned PaymentLineItems bug.

followUps.question: Why does @@IDENTITY fail when triggers are involved?
followUps.answer:
Definition: @@IDENTITY returns the last identity value generated in the current session across all scopes including triggers. When an AFTER INSERT trigger on the base table inserts into another table that also has an identity column, @@IDENTITY changes to that trigger table's identity value. SCOPE_IDENTITY() is immune because it tracks identity values only in the current T-SQL scope — trigger execution occurs in a nested scope that is invisible to SCOPE_IDENTITY().

Advantages:

  • SCOPE_IDENTITY() works correctly regardless of how many triggers exist on the table — trigger identity values never pollute it
  • The failure mode of @@IDENTITY is silent — it returns a valid-looking integer that happens to be wrong — making it particularly dangerous in production systems
  • Understanding scope boundaries explains why SCOPE_IDENTITY() is the universal recommendation over @@IDENTITY for all new SQL Server code

Fintech Example: A loan origination procedure used @@IDENTITY to get the LoanId after INSERT. An audit trigger on Loans also inserted into a LoanAuditTrail table. In development without the trigger, @@IDENTITY worked correctly. After deploying the audit trigger to production, @@IDENTITY started returning LoanAuditTrail identity values — loan documents were attached to non-existent loan IDs. SCOPE_IDENTITY() fixed the issue immediately.

followUps.question: What is the OUTPUT clause and how is it better than SCOPE_IDENTITY()?
followUps.answer:
Definition: The OUTPUT clause captures values from rows affected by INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or MERGE and returns them as a result set or inserts them into a table variable. Unlike SCOPE_IDENTITY() which returns only the last identity from a single-row INSERT, OUTPUT captures all generated values from multi-row INSERT operations — making it the correct choice for bulk inserts requiring all generated IDs.

Advantages:

  • Captures all generated identity values from multi-row inserts — SCOPE_IDENTITY() only returns the last one
  • For UPDATE and DELETE, OUTPUT captures both INSERTED (new values) and DELETED (old values) in the same statement — enabling atomic change capture
  • OUTPUT is atomic with the DML — no race condition between the INSERT and reading the identity, unlike reading SCOPE_IDENTITY() after a separate SELECT

Fintech Example: A batch payment creation procedure inserts multiple Payment rows and needs all generated PaymentIds to create corresponding PaymentAuditEntry records. Using INSERT INTO Payments OUTPUT INSERTED.PaymentId INTO @GeneratedIds SELECT * FROM @PaymentBatch captures all IDs atomically. SCOPE_IDENTITY() would only return the last PaymentId — missing all but one ID from the batch insert.

questions.tip: Default choice: always SCOPE_IDENTITY() for single-row inserts. For multi-row inserts or when you need the full inserted data, use the OUTPUT clause. Never use @@IDENTITY if there are AFTER INSERT triggers on the table. Never use IDENT_CURRENT() in multi-user environments — it's not session-scoped.

questions.question: What is the difference between OLTP and OLAP? How do they affect database design?
questions.answer:
Definition: OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) is optimised for short, frequent read/write operations on current data — order placement, payment processing, account updates. OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) is optimised for complex analytical queries over large historical datasets — revenue reports, trend analysis, business intelligence. They require fundamentally different schema designs, indexing strategies, and hardware configurations.

Advantages:

  • Normalised OLTP schemas minimise write anomalies and enforce data integrity — critical for financial transaction correctness
  • Denormalised OLAP star schemas with columnstore indexes enable aggregations over billions of rows in seconds — impossible on normalised OLTP schemas
  • Separating OLTP and OLAP workloads prevents analytical queries from blocking transactional processing — keeping payment latency unaffected by reporting load

Fintech Example: A payment platform uses a normalised SQL Server OLTP database for real-time transaction processing (sub-millisecond balance checks, instant payment inserts) and a separate Azure Synapse OLAP data warehouse for business intelligence (daily ETL loads, monthly revenue reports, regulatory capital calculations). The two systems are never on the same server — OLAP query load cannot impact OLTP transaction throughput.

followUps.question: What is a Data Warehouse and how does it relate to OLAP?
followUps.answer:
Definition: A data warehouse is a centralised repository optimised for OLAP — storing integrated historical data from multiple OLTP source systems, cleaned and transformed via ETL (Extract, Transform, Load). Data warehouses use star schemas (central fact table surrounded by dimension tables) that are deliberately denormalised for fast aggregation reads. Columnstore indexes enable vectorised compression and sub-second aggregations over billions of rows.

Advantages:

  • Consolidates data from multiple operational systems into a single analytical platform — cross-system reporting impossible in normalised OLTP schemas
  • Historical point-in-time data preserved regardless of OLTP changes — dimension slowly changing history (SCD) tracks how customer attributes changed over time
  • Columnstore indexes on fact tables achieve 5–10x compression and 100x faster aggregations compared to row-store indexes on the same data

Fintech Example: A banking group's data warehouse consolidates transaction data from retail banking, mortgages, and investment systems into a single star schema. The fact_transaction table has 5 billion rows with a columnstore index — monthly regulatory capital calculations that previously ran overnight on OLTP systems complete in under 10 minutes on the warehouse, using vectorised aggregation across all product lines simultaneously.

followUps.question: What is HTAP (Hybrid Transactional/Analytical Processing)?
followUps.answer:
Definition: HTAP (Hybrid Transactional/Analytical Processing) combines OLTP and OLAP workloads in a single system, enabling real-time analytics on current operational data without a separate ETL pipeline. SQL Server achieves HTAP by adding a non-clustered columnstore index to a row-store OLTP table — OLTP writes use row storage while analytical queries use the columnstore, both maintained automatically.

Advantages:

  • Eliminates ETL delay — analytics are based on data written milliseconds ago, not hours-old ETL loads
  • No separate analytical infrastructure required — reduces operational complexity and cost compared to maintaining both OLTP and OLAP systems
  • The columnstore is an updateable non-clustered index — OLTP INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE performance is slightly affected but remains viable for moderate write workloads

Fintech Example: A real-time fraud scoring system needs sub-second analytical queries (merchant velocity checks, amount deviation from baseline) on the live Transactions table while simultaneously processing high-volume payment inserts. Adding a non-clustered columnstore index to Transactions enables the fraud queries to use vectorised aggregation on current data — eliminating the 15-minute ETL lag that previously made the fraud model operate on stale transaction patterns.

questions.tip: Key distinction for interviews: OLTP = many small fast transactions, normalised schema, optimise writes. OLAP = few large complex queries, denormalised star schema, optimise reads. Your day-to-day application databases are OLTP. Reporting/BI databases are OLAP. A data warehouse is an OLAP system fed by ETL from OLTP systems.

questions.question: What is index fragmentation in SQL Server and how do you fix it?
questions.answer:
Definition: Index fragmentation occurs when the logical order of index pages no longer matches physical storage order (external fragmentation) or when pages are sparsely populated from deletions (internal fragmentation). It forces additional I/O and prevents efficient sequential reads. Fragmentation accumulates naturally as data is inserted, updated, and deleted. The fix is REORGANIZE for 10–30% fragmentation or REBUILD for over 30%.

Advantages:

  • REORGANIZE is an online operation with minimal blocking — appropriate for production systems that cannot tolerate maintenance window downtime
  • REBUILD (with ONLINE = ON in Enterprise Edition) fully defragments the index and updates statistics simultaneously — two maintenance tasks in one operation
  • Monitoring via sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats before and after maintenance validates that the operation achieved the expected fragmentation reduction

Fintech Example: A payment processing database with a high-churn Transactions table (5 million inserts and deletes daily) showed 70% external fragmentation within 48 hours of the last REBUILD. Settlement queries ran 3x slower due to random I/O. An automated nightly maintenance job using Ola Hallengren's IndexOptimize script (REBUILD above 30%, REORGANIZE between 10–30%) kept fragmentation below 15% indefinitely, maintaining consistent settlement query performance.

followUps.question: What is Fill Factor and how does it relate to fragmentation?
followUps.answer:
Definition: Fill Factor specifies the percentage of each index leaf page to fill during index BUILD or REBUILD. The default (0, treated as 100%) fills pages completely. When new rows must be inserted between existing rows and the page is full, SQL Server performs a page split — writing half the rows to a new page. This immediately creates fragmentation and is expensive. A lower Fill Factor leaves free space to absorb inserts before splits occur.

Advantages:

  • A Fill Factor of 80% reduces page split frequency by leaving 20% free space — inserts use the slack before a split is needed, slowing fragmentation accumulation
  • Append-only tables (monotonically increasing keys like INT IDENTITY) benefit from 100% Fill Factor — inserts never go in the middle, splits never occur regardless of Fill Factor
  • Balancing Fill Factor against the write pattern minimises total maintenance overhead — too low wastes space and read I/O, too high causes frequent splits and REBUILD requirements

Fintech Example: An order management table using GUID primary keys experienced constant page splits at 100% Fill Factor because each GUID INSERT lands in a random position in the index. Setting FILLFACTOR=70 during REBUILD left sufficient slack to absorb several weeks of inserts before fragmentation reached the REBUILD threshold — reducing weekly REBUILD frequency to monthly.

followUps.question: How do you automate index maintenance in SQL Server?
followUps.answer:
Definition: Index maintenance automation schedules REORGANIZE or REBUILD operations based on measured fragmentation levels. Options include SQL Server Agent jobs running custom T-SQL, Ola Hallengren's widely-used IndexOptimize maintenance solution, SSMS Maintenance Plans, and Azure SQL Database's built-in Automatic Tuning (auto-manages indexes and statistics without manual configuration).

Advantages:

  • Scheduled maintenance prevents fragmentation from silently accumulating to levels that cause significant query degradation between planned maintenance windows
  • Threshold-based automation (REORGANIZE below 30%, REBUILD above) applies the minimum necessary operation — reducing I/O and lock duration compared to always rebuilding all indexes
  • Ola Hallengren's solution is production-battle-tested, free, and handles edge cases (system databases, replicated tables, partition-aware maintenance) out of the box

Fintech Example: A payment platform's SQL Server Agent runs Ola Hallengren's IndexOptimize every Sunday at 2 AM — REBUILD indexes above 30% fragmentation with FILLFACTOR=80, REORGANIZE between 10–30%, skip indexes with fewer than 1,000 pages. The automated run produces a log showing which indexes were rebuilt, ensuring the settlements team has consistently fast query performance at the start of each new week.

questions.tip: Thresholds to remember: < 5% → do nothing. 5–30% → REORGANIZE (online, low impact). > 30% → REBUILD (higher impact, fully defragments). Check fragmentation with sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats. Fill Factor leaves intentional free space to delay future fragmentation — lower for write-heavy, higher for read-heavy tables.

questions.question: How do you delete duplicate rows in SQL Server while keeping one copy?
questions.answer:
Definition: The cleanest approach to deleting duplicate rows uses ROW_NUMBER() inside a CTE to assign a sequential number within each duplicate group, then deletes all rows where the number is greater than 1 (keeping only the first occurrence per group). The PARTITION BY clause defines which columns determine "duplicate" and ORDER BY determines which copy to keep.

Advantages:

  • Deleting directly from a CTE with ROW_NUMBER() is set-based and works in a single statement — no temp tables or multiple passes required
  • Replacing DELETE with SELECT * in the CTE previews exactly which rows will be removed before committing — essential for safety in production
  • PARTITION BY flexibility allows defining duplicates at any granularity — exact row duplicates or business-key duplicates on specific columns

Fintech Example: A payment import process accidentally created duplicate transaction records when a batch file was processed twice. The CTE duplicate deletion: WITH Dupes AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ExternalRef, Amount, MerchantId ORDER BY CreatedAt) AS rn FROM Transactions) DELETE FROM Dupes WHERE rn > 1 — keeping the earliest insert for each duplicate group. Running SELECT first confirmed exactly 15,247 duplicate rows would be removed before executing the DELETE.

followUps.question: How do you find duplicates without deleting them?
followUps.answer:
Definition: Finding duplicates without deleting uses GROUP BY with HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 to identify duplicate groups, or a subquery/CTE with ROW_NUMBER() to show all individual duplicate rows with their row numbers. The GROUP BY approach shows which values are duplicated and how many times; the ROW_NUMBER() approach shows all the individual rows that form each duplicate group.

Advantages:

  • GROUP BY HAVING gives a quick summary — how many distinct duplicate values exist and their frequency counts — without listing every individual duplicate row
  • ROW_NUMBER() approach shows all individual duplicate rows with context — enabling review of which rows to keep before executing the deletion
  • Running the find query in a transaction and reviewing results before committing the delete is standard safe practice for production duplicate cleanup

Fintech Example: Before a duplicate payment cleanup, the team ran SELECT ExternalRef, COUNT(*) AS Count, MIN(CreatedAt) AS First, MAX(CreatedAt) AS Last FROM Payments GROUP BY ExternalRef HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 ORDER BY Count DESC — revealing 3,200 duplicate groups, the largest with 5 copies of the same payment. This summary guided the investigation (all duplicates were from a specific import window) before executing the deletion with confidence.

questions.tip: Always preview first: Replace DELETE with SELECT * in the CTE method to see exactly which rows will be removed. Wrap in a transaction with ROLLBACK until you're confident.

questions.question: How do you optimise a slow SQL query or stored procedure?
questions.answer:
Definition: Query and stored procedure optimisation follows a systematic process: first examine the actual execution plan to identify the most expensive operators (table scans, key lookups, sort operators), add targeted indexes to eliminate scans, rewrite non-sargable conditions (functions on indexed columns), replace correlated subqueries with JOINs, address parameter sniffing with OPTION hints, and update stale statistics.

Advantages:

  • Execution plan analysis identifies the root cause objectively — eliminating guesswork and focusing effort on the actual bottleneck
  • Adding a covering index on the right columns often provides a 10–100x improvement with no query rewrite required
  • Fixing non-sargable conditions (rewriting YEAR(date) as date range) restores index seeks with zero schema changes

Fintech Example: A slow merchant settlement report was profiled with SET STATISTICS IO ON, revealing 45,000 logical reads and a Key Lookup operator with 92% plan cost. The key lookup fetched Amount and Description for each row after seeking on (MerchantId, Status). Adding INCLUDE (Amount, Description) to the existing index eliminated all key lookups, reducing logical reads from 45,000 to 380 and report generation time from 8 minutes to 25 seconds.

followUps.question: What is parameter sniffing in SQL Server?
followUps.answer:
Definition: Parameter sniffing is SQL Server's behaviour of compiling a stored procedure's execution plan using the first parameter values supplied, then caching and reusing that plan for all subsequent calls. When the first call uses atypical parameters (e.g., a very selective value returning 5 rows), the cached plan may be disastrously wrong for subsequent calls with common parameters (returning 500,000 rows).

Advantages:

  • Identifying parameter sniffing as the root cause explains procedure performance that appears to fix itself after SQL Server restart (plan cache cleared) then degrades again
  • OPTION (RECOMPILE) produces an optimal plan per call — appropriate for procedures where the performance difference between plans is extreme
  • OPTION (OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN) uses average statistics for a balanced plan — appropriate when the performance difference is moderate and consistent throughput is preferred over per-call optimality

Fintech Example: A client portfolio query procedure was first called with a VIP client's ID (2 million transactions — table scan optimal), caching a scan plan. All calls for smaller clients (average 200 transactions — index seek optimal) reused the scan plan, causing 8-second queries that should take 40ms. Adding OPTION (OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN) produced a balanced index seek plan that performed acceptably for all client sizes.

questions.tip: Start with the execution plan. 80% of query performance issues are solved by adding an index on the right column. Look for Table Scans first.

questions.question: What is the difference between a stored procedure and a function in SQL Server?
questions.answer:
Definition: A stored procedure is a named T-SQL block executed with EXEC, can perform DML, manage transactions, use input/output parameters, and return multiple result sets. A function must return a value or table, is called within SQL expressions (SELECT, WHERE, JOIN), cannot perform DML, and cannot manage transactions. Functions are for pure computation; procedures are for business logic with data modification.

Advantages:

  • Functions are composable — usable in SELECT, WHERE, JOIN, and computed columns, enabling reuse in complex queries
  • Stored procedures handle complex workflows requiring transactions, conditional DML, and output parameters — the correct tool for multi-step business operations
  • Inline TVFs (table-valued functions with a single RETURN SELECT) are inlined by the optimizer, providing function composability with view-level performance

Fintech Example: A payment system uses a dbo.CalculateLateFee(@dueDate, @amount) scalar function in SELECT queries across multiple reports — callable anywhere a scalar expression is valid. The actual fee assessment (INSERT into FeeAssessments, UPDATE AccountBalance) is done by uspAssessLateFee stored procedure — it calls the function for the calculation, then performs the DML. Functions compute; procedures act.

followUps.question: What is the difference between a scalar function and a table-valued function (TVF)?
followUps.answer:
Definition: A scalar function returns a single value and is called once per row when used in SELECT or WHERE — on large tables, this per-row invocation creates significant performance overhead. An inline table-valued function (iTVF) uses a single RETURN SELECT with no BEGIN/END — the optimizer inlines its definition into the calling query's plan, enabling full optimisation including index seeks. A multi-statement TVF uses BEGIN/END and is opaque to the optimizer, producing poor cardinality estimates.

Advantages:

  • iTVFs perform identically to views from an optimisation standpoint — they participate in the calling query's full plan optimisation
  • Scalar functions in WHERE clauses are non-sargable and prevent index use — replacing them with inline expressions or iTVFs restores index seeks
  • Avoid multi-statement TVFs for performance-critical queries — the optimizer's inability to look inside them leads to poor plan choices for the calling query

Fintech Example: A risk scoring query used a scalar function dbo.GetMerchantRiskScore(MerchantId) in a WHERE clause — executing once per row for 500,000 merchants and causing a 45-second query. Rewriting as an inline TVF that the optimizer merged into the main query plan reduced execution to 3 seconds by enabling parallel execution and index seeks on the risk score calculation's underlying tables.

questions.tip: Rule of thumb: If you need to encapsulate logic and reuse it in a SELECT, use a TVF. If you need to perform data modifications (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) or complex logic, use a stored procedure.

questions.question: Write a SQL query to count the number of employees in each department.
questions.answer:
Definition: Counting employees per department is a standard GROUP BY aggregation query combining a JOIN (to get department names) with COUNT(), GROUP BY, and optionally HAVING for filtering groups. LEFT JOIN is essential to include departments with zero employees that INNER JOIN would exclude.

Advantages:

  • GROUP BY with COUNT() produces one result row per department in a single query pass — far more efficient than N separate SELECT COUNT(*) queries
  • LEFT JOIN preserves departments with no employees — critical for reporting that must account for all departments including empty ones
  • Adding aggregate functions (AVG, MAX, MIN salary) alongside COUNT() computes multiple department statistics in the same single-pass query

Fintech Example: HR analytics query for regulatory headcount reporting: SELECT d.DepartmentName, COUNT(e.EmployeeId) AS Headcount, AVG(e.Salary) AS AvgSalary FROM Departments d LEFT JOIN Employees e ON e.DepartmentId = d.DepartmentId GROUP BY d.DepartmentId, d.DepartmentName ORDER BY Headcount DESC. LEFT JOIN ensures compliance, risk, and audit departments with only contractors (not in the Employees table) still appear with zero headcount in the regulatory submission.

followUps.question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING in this context?
followUps.answer:
Definition: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping — it cannot reference aggregate functions and applies to the raw data. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY — it can reference aggregate functions and applies to the aggregated result. Using WHERE for non-aggregate conditions and HAVING for aggregate conditions is both semantically correct and more efficient.

Advantages:

  • WHERE reduces the row set before GROUP BY processes it — fewer rows to aggregate means faster query execution on large tables
  • HAVING enables conditions impossible with WHERE — finding departments where average salary exceeds a threshold requires the aggregate to be computed first
  • Combining both in one query provides two-stage filtering: row-level exclusion via WHERE, then group-level exclusion via HAVING

Fintech Example: A compensation analysis query filters full-time employees (WHERE EmploymentType = 'Full-Time' — row-level) then finds departments where total payroll exceeds the budget threshold (HAVING SUM(Salary) > 5000000 — group-level). WHERE eliminates contractors from the aggregation; HAVING identifies over-budget departments. Both filters serve different purposes and cannot substitute for each other.

questions.tip: Use LEFT JOIN (not INNER JOIN) when listing departments with counts — INNER JOIN would exclude departments with zero employees. If you want zero-employee departments to appear in the list, LEFT JOIN is essential.

questions.question: What is denormalization? When do you intentionally break normal form?
questions.answer:
Definition: Denormalisation deliberately reintroduces data redundancy to improve query performance. It trades write complexity (maintaining redundant data consistently) for read speed (fewer joins, pre-computed aggregates). Valid scenarios include OLAP reporting schemas, pre-computed aggregate columns, CQRS read model projections, and data warehouse star schemas.

Advantages:

  • Pre-joining data eliminates runtime join overhead on hot read paths — a denormalised read model table can serve dashboard queries with a single scan
  • Pre-computed columns (Order.TotalAmount) avoid recalculating from child rows on every read — critical for high-frequency balance and summary displays
  • Star schema denormalisation in data warehouses enables columnstore compression and vectorised aggregation across billions of rows

Fintech Example: A portfolio valuation dashboard querying 8 normalised tables for every page load was too slow under concurrent users. A CQRS PortfolioSummaryView read model — denormalised, pre-joined, rebuilt on each trade event via a domain event handler — reduced dashboard load from 2.5 seconds to 35ms. The write schema stayed normalised; only the read model was denormalised.

followUps.question: What is the difference between OLTP and OLAP database design?
followUps.answer:
Definition: OLTP databases are normalised (3NF+), optimised for low-latency individual row reads and writes, with many targeted indexes and strict transaction integrity. OLAP databases are intentionally denormalised (star/snowflake schema), optimised for large-scale aggregation queries with columnstore indexes, designed for reading historical data across millions to billions of rows.

Advantages:

  • OLTP normalisation prevents update anomalies and ensures transactional correctness — essential for financial data integrity
  • OLAP denormalisation with star schemas and columnstore indexes enables sub-second aggregations that normalised schemas cannot achieve at scale
  • Maintaining separate OLTP and OLAP systems prevents analytical workloads from degrading transactional performance — each system optimised independently

Fintech Example: A bank's core banking system uses a normalised SQL Server OLTP database — 3NF schema, row-store indexes, every write within ACID transactions. The business intelligence platform uses Azure Synapse Analytics — star schema with fact_transaction at the centre, dimension tables for date, merchant, product, and geography, columnstore indexes on all facts. The two systems serve completely different query patterns and are never on the same infrastructure.

questions.tip: CQRS + read models is the modern approach. Instead of denormalising your transactional tables (which creates data consistency headaches), create separate read-optimised projections. Your write model stays clean; your read model is optimised for queries.

questions.question: What is SQL Server Connection Pooling? How does it work and what are the pitfalls?
questions.answer:
Definition: Connection pooling reuses existing database connections rather than creating a new physical connection on every request. ADO.NET manages a pool per unique connection string — conn.Open() retrieves a pooled connection if available, conn.Dispose() (via using) returns it to the pool rather than closing it. Pool size defaults to min=0, max=100 connections per connection string.

Advantages:

  • Eliminates connection establishment overhead — opening a new physical SQL Server connection takes 10–50ms; reusing a pooled connection takes microseconds
  • Limits total connections to SQL Server — prevents a traffic spike from exhausting SQL Server's connection capacity (max 32,767 connections)
  • Connection lifecycle management is automatic — ADO.NET handles pool creation, growth, pruning, and health checking without application code

Fintech Example: A payment API under load testing was creating a new SQL Server connection for each of 1,000 concurrent requests — connection establishment added 40ms per request and SQL Server quickly exhausted its connection limit. Ensuring all SqlConnection objects were in using blocks enabled pool reuse, reducing average connection overhead to under 0.1ms and allowing the same 1,000 concurrent requests to share a pool of 100 physical connections.

followUps.question: How does changing a connection string affect pooling?
followUps.answer:
Definition: ADO.NET connection pools are keyed on the exact connection string — every unique string gets its own separate pool. Changing any connection string property (username, password, server, database, or even whitespace) creates a new pool rather than reusing the existing one. In multi-tenant applications where each tenant uses a different connection string, this creates N separate pools — one per tenant.

Advantages:

  • Per-connection-string pooling provides natural tenant isolation — one tenant's connection exhaustion cannot affect another tenant's pool
  • Consistent connection string construction (same property order, same whitespace) ensures the same pool is reused rather than accidentally creating duplicate pools
  • Dynamic connection strings from configuration can be normalised (sorted properties, trimmed whitespace) to prevent unintended pool fragmentation

Fintech Example: A multi-tenant SaaS platform with 200 clients each using their own database user created 200 separate connection pools when connection strings were built with varying property order (sometimes "User Id" first, sometimes "Password" first). Standardising connection string construction to a canonical property order collapsed the fragmented pools into correct per-tenant pools, reducing total open SQL Server connections from 4,000 to 800.

questions.tip: Always use 'using' for SqlConnection. This is the single most important rule. Connection leaks are insidious — the app works fine under low load and mysteriously breaks under traffic spikes.

questions.question: What are subqueries in SQL? What is the difference between a correlated and non-correlated subquery?
questions.answer:
Definition: A subquery is a query nested inside another query. A non-correlated subquery runs once independently of the outer query — its result is computed once and reused. A correlated subquery references columns from the outer query, causing it to re-execute once for every row processed by the outer query — potentially making it O(n) times slower than the equivalent JOIN or CTE approach.

Advantages:

  • Non-correlated subqueries are often interchangeable with JOINs and provide equivalent performance — use whichever is more readable
  • EXISTS with a correlated subquery short-circuits at the first match — more efficient than IN for large subquery results
  • CTEs replace deeply nested subqueries with named, readable steps — the same result with dramatically better maintainability

Fintech Example: A query finding accounts with transactions above the account's own average: SELECT AccountId, Amount FROM Transactions t WHERE Amount > (SELECT AVG(Amount) FROM Transactions WHERE AccountId = t.AccountId) — a correlated subquery executing once per row. Rewriting with a CTE that computes averages once per account and JOINs back reduces execution from O(n) subquery calls to a single aggregation pass, cutting query time from 45 seconds to 2 seconds on 10 million rows.

followUps.question: Why can correlated subqueries be a performance problem?
followUps.answer:
Definition: A correlated subquery re-executes for every row processed by the outer query because it references the outer query's columns. If the outer query returns 10,000 rows, the correlated subquery runs 10,000 times. For large tables, this produces O(n×m) complexity — the same work that a single GROUP BY aggregation or JOIN would do in O(n+m).

Advantages:

  • Rewriting as a CTE with GROUP BY computes the subquery result once rather than once per row — a single pass replaces N passes
  • The execution plan reveals correlated subquery cost — a Nested Loop with high estimated rows on the inner side signals the pattern and its cost
  • EXISTS is the one case where correlation is acceptable — it short-circuits at the first match, often examining very few rows before returning

Fintech Example: A fraud risk query checked whether each transaction's amount exceeded the merchant's average by 3x using a correlated subquery — executing the AVG() subquery once per transaction for 5 million daily transactions. Rewriting as WITH MerchantAvg AS (SELECT MerchantId, AVG(Amount)*3 AS Threshold FROM Transactions GROUP BY MerchantId) SELECT t.* FROM Transactions t JOIN MerchantAvg m ON t.MerchantId = m.MerchantId WHERE t.Amount > m.Threshold reduced execution from 3 minutes to 8 seconds.

questions.tip: EXISTS over IN for safety. IN with a subquery that can return NULLs will silently return zero rows — a hard bug to track down. EXISTS never has this issue. Also, EXISTS short-circuits at the first match, making it faster for large sets.

questions.question: What are constraints in SQL? Explain all types with examples.
questions.answer:
Definition: SQL constraints are rules enforced at the database level to ensure data integrity. The six types are: PRIMARY KEY (uniquely identifies each row, no NULL), FOREIGN KEY (enforces referential integrity between tables), UNIQUE (unique values per column, allows one NULL), NOT NULL (column must always have a value), CHECK (validates values against an expression), and DEFAULT (provides a default value when none is specified).

Advantages:

  • Database-level enforcement is the last line of defence — constraints catch data integrity violations even when application-level validation has bugs
  • Named constraints are manageable — explicitly named constraints (CHK_Price, UQ_Email) can be referenced in ALTER TABLE DROP CONSTRAINT statements and migration scripts
  • CHECK constraints on status columns (CHECK (Status IN ('Pending', 'Completed', 'Failed'))) prevent invalid state values from application bugs reaching the database

Fintech Example: A payment table has CHECK (Amount > 0) — rejecting zero or negative payment amounts at the database level. A bug in the payment calculation service returned zero for a specific edge case. The CHECK constraint rejected the INSERT with a clear error rather than silently inserting a £0.00 payment, surfacing the calculation bug before it affected account balances. Application validation is the first line; database constraints are the last.

followUps.question: What is the difference between PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE constraint?
followUps.answer:
Definition: A PRIMARY KEY constraint uniquely identifies each row, prohibits NULL values, allows only one per table, and by default creates a clustered index. A UNIQUE constraint also enforces uniqueness but allows one NULL value (because NULL is unknown — two unknown values are not considered equal in SQL Server's implementation), allows multiple per table, and creates a non-clustered index by default.

Advantages:

  • PRIMARY KEY defines the entity's system identifier used as the target of all foreign key references — the central node in the schema's relationship graph
  • UNIQUE constraints enforce business-level uniqueness on additional columns (email, account number, passport number) without consuming the single PRIMARY KEY slot
  • The clustered index created by the default PRIMARY KEY determines physical row order — choosing the right PK impacts the entire table's read access pattern

Fintech Example: An Accounts table has AccountId INT IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY (system identifier — never null, drives clustered index physical order, all FKs reference this) and AccountNumber NVARCHAR(20) UNIQUE NOT NULL (business identifier — unique per regulatory requirement, assigned during account creation). Both enforce uniqueness but serve different purposes and reference different aspects of the account entity.

questions.tip: Name all your constraints. AUTO-named constraints (SQL Server generates names like 'DF__Orders__Status__3B75D760') are hard to drop and manage in migrations. Always give them explicit names: CHK_Price, UQ_Email, FK_Orders_Customers. Your future self will thank you.

questions.question: What are the types of database relationships? Explain one-to-one, one-to-many, and many-to-many.
questions.answer:
Definition: Database relationships define how tables relate to each other. One-to-one (1:1) maps each row in Table A to at most one row in Table B — enforced via a UNIQUE constraint on the FK. One-to-many (1:N) is the most common: one row in Table A can have many rows in Table B — the FK goes on the many side. Many-to-many (M:N) requires a junction table to break it into two 1:N relationships.

Advantages:

  • One-to-many with FK on the child table is the simplest and most queryable relationship structure — joining parent to children is straightforward with standard JOINs
  • Junction tables for many-to-many relationships can carry additional relationship attributes (enrollment date, role, status) that belong to the relationship itself, not either entity
  • One-to-one relationships enable table-level security partitioning — sensitive data in a separate table with tighter permissions than the main entity table

Fintech Example: A loan management system has Customer (1) to Loans (many) — one customer can have multiple loans. A many-to-many between Loans and Collateral items uses a LoanCollateral junction table that stores the lien_percentage column — data that belongs to the relationship, not either entity. A one-to-one between Customer and CustomerKYCProfile separates sensitive identity verification data (passport numbers, biometric hashes) from the main customer table with tighter database permissions on the KYC table.

followUps.question: How do you implement many-to-many in EF Core?
followUps.answer:
Definition: EF Core supports many-to-many either implicitly (EF Core 5+ automatic junction table with skip navigations) or explicitly (define the join entity class with extra columns). Implicit many-to-many uses skip navigations (student.Courses, course.Students) with EF Core managing the junction table. Explicit join entities are required when the junction table carries additional data like enrollment date or approval status.

Advantages:

  • Skip navigations let you traverse student.Courses directly without manually joining through the junction entity in LINQ queries
  • Explicit join entities allow storing relationship metadata (EnrolledOn, Grade, ApprovalStatus) that belongs to the association, not either end entity
  • EF Core handles cascade deletes and FK constraints for the junction table automatically when configured via Fluent API

Fintech Example: A loan management system has a many-to-many between Borrowers and LoanProducts. The junction entity BorrowerProductApplication stores ApplicationDate and ApprovalStatus — data that belongs to the specific borrower-product combination. Configuring with modelBuilder.Entity<BorrowerProductApplication>().HasKey(b => new { b.BorrowerId, b.ProductId }) and HasOne/HasMany on each side gives full EF Core navigation support including skip navigations.

followUps.question: What is a composite primary key?
followUps.answer:
Definition: A composite primary key consists of two or more columns whose combined values uniquely identify each row. Neither column alone needs to be unique — it is the combination that must be. In SQL Server, composite PKs are defined with PRIMARY KEY (ColA, ColB) syntax. In EF Core, composite PKs are configured exclusively via Fluent API: HasKey(e => new { e.ColA, e.ColB }) — data annotations do not support composite keys.

Advantages:

  • Natural fit for junction tables — (StudentId, CourseId) composite PK prevents the same student from enrolling in the same course twice at the schema level
  • Eliminates the need for a surrogate identity column on tables where a natural composite key is stable and meaningful
  • Enforces business-level uniqueness constraints directly in the schema rather than relying solely on application validation or add-on UNIQUE indexes

Fintech Example: A WalletTransactionLedger table uses composite PK (WalletId, TransactionId) — the same transaction can only be posted once per wallet. A reconciliation bug that attempted to post the same transaction twice to the same wallet was caught immediately by the PK violation rather than creating duplicate ledger entries that would silently inflate the wallet balance.

followUps.question: When would you use a one-to-one relationship instead of putting everything in one table?
followUps.answer:
Definition: A one-to-one relationship splits data belonging to the same conceptual entity into two separate tables, linked by a FK with a UNIQUE constraint on the dependent side. Common reasons: separating rarely-accessed large columns from frequently-queried columns, enforcing tighter table-level security on sensitive data, or modelling optional extension data that only some entities have.

Advantages:

  • Keeps the main table narrow and its data pages lean — frequently-queried queries don't load large optional columns they don't need
  • Enables table-level permission separation — sensitive supplementary data (KYC details, biometrics) in a separate table with restricted permissions
  • Models optional extension data cleanly — a User may or may not have a UserKycProfile, which is cleaner than NULLable columns in the User table

Fintech Example: Every Customer row is lean (ID, name, email, status). KYC verification details (passport number, verified date, risk score, document scan path) live in a separate CustomerKycDetail table linked one-to-one. Only the compliance microservice's database user has SELECT permission on CustomerKycDetail — the main application reads from Customer freely without accessing regulated identity data, satisfying data minimisation requirements under GDPR.

questions.tip: For many-to-many, always create a named junction entity in EF Core if the relationship has extra data.

questions.question: What is SET NOCOUNT ON/OFF in SQL Server? When should you use it?
questions.answer:
Definition: SET NOCOUNT ON suppresses the "N row(s) affected" messages SQL Server sends back to the client after each DML statement. Without it, every INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE in a stored procedure sends an extra network message. In ORM contexts, these row-count messages can interfere with EF Core's optimistic concurrency checking which relies on the rows-affected count from the final DML statement.

Advantages:

  • Reduces network traffic — stored procedures with multiple DML statements generate multiple row-count messages without NOCOUNT ON
  • Prevents false EF Core DbUpdateConcurrencyException errors caused by trigger DML returning unexpected extra row counts
  • Considered best practice for all stored procedures — including it consistently prevents subtle ORM integration bugs across the entire codebase

Fintech Example: An EF Core payment application was randomly throwing DbUpdateConcurrencyException on payment updates. Investigation revealed an AFTER UPDATE trigger on Payments inserting audit rows without SET NOCOUNT ON — EF Core received a rows-affected count of 2 instead of the expected 1 and incorrectly interpreted it as a concurrency conflict. Adding SET NOCOUNT ON to the trigger resolved all false exceptions immediately.

followUps.question: How is @@ROWCOUNT affected by SET NOCOUNT ON?
followUps.answer:
Definition: @@ROWCOUNT stores the number of rows affected by the most recent statement. SET NOCOUNT ON suppresses only the network message sent to the client — it does NOT affect the value stored in @@ROWCOUNT. After any DML statement in a stored procedure with SET NOCOUNT ON, @@ROWCOUNT still correctly reflects the number of rows affected by that specific statement.

Advantages:

  • SET NOCOUNT ON can be safely combined with @@ROWCOUNT-based validation logic — the two settings are independent
  • @@ROWCOUNT checked immediately after an UPDATE or DELETE correctly detects whether any rows matched the condition — a common pattern for detecting stale or missing records
  • The separation clarifies that NOCOUNT is a network communication setting, not a data access setting

Fintech Example: A payment instruction stored procedure uses SET NOCOUNT ON at the top for performance, then checks IF @@ROWCOUNT = 0 THROW 50001, 'Payment instruction not found', 1 after updating a PaymentInstruction row. If no row matched (stale ID or concurrent delete), @@ROWCOUNT is 0 and the error is raised. The NOCOUNT setting does not interfere — @@ROWCOUNT still correctly reflects the UPDATE's affected row count.

followUps.question: What is SET XACT_ABORT ON and when do you use it?
followUps.answer:
Definition: SET XACT_ABORT ON instructs SQL Server to automatically roll back the entire current transaction and terminate the batch if any statement raises a runtime error. Without it, a runtime error may abort only the individual statement while leaving the transaction open in a partially-modified state — a common source of data integrity bugs when error handling is incomplete.

Advantages:

  • Guarantees atomic transaction rollback on any unhandled error — eliminates the class of bugs where a partial transaction is left open due to incomplete CATCH block coverage
  • Simplifies stored procedure error handling — XACT_ABORT handles errors automatically, reducing the need for manual IF @@TRANCOUNT > 0 ROLLBACK checks
  • Works correctly with linked servers and distributed transactions where partial failures would otherwise leave distributed locks held indefinitely

Fintech Example: A funds transfer procedure that debits one account and credits another uses SET XACT_ABORT ON. If the credit UPDATE fails due to a CHECK constraint (account frozen), XACT_ABORT immediately rolls back the entire transaction — including the already-executed debit. Without XACT_ABORT, the debit could persist while the credit fails, causing money to vanish from the source account without appearing in the destination.

followUps.question: Does SET NOCOUNT ON improve performance significantly?
followUps.answer:
Definition: The performance benefit of SET NOCOUNT ON comes from eliminating the "N row(s) affected" network message after each DML statement. The gain is proportional to the number of DML statements in the procedure — negligible for single-statement procedures but measurable for procedures executing many statements in loops or batch operations called thousands of times per second.

Advantages:

  • Measurable improvement in stored procedures with cursor-based or loop processing executing many DML statements per call
  • Prevents ORM interference — EF Core reads rows-affected counts; extra messages from trigger DML cause false DbUpdateConcurrencyException errors
  • Zero downside — no SQL Server functionality is affected by SET NOCOUNT ON, making it a cost-free best practice for all stored procedures

Fintech Example: A nightly reconciliation stored procedure processing 50,000 payment rows one-by-one (legacy cursor design) was generating 50,000 "1 row affected" network messages without NOCOUNT ON. Adding SET NOCOUNT ON reduced procedure runtime from 8 minutes to 6.5 minutes — a 19% improvement purely from eliminating 50,000 network round-trips, without changing any of the business logic.

questions.tip: Always add SET NOCOUNT ON at the top of stored procedures — it's a best practice question.

questions.question: What is RAISERROR in SQL Server? How does it differ from THROW?
questions.answer:
Definition: RAISERROR is the legacy T-SQL error statement (SQL Server 2000+) raising errors with explicit severity and state parameters. THROW is the modern replacement (SQL Server 2012+) with simpler syntax. The key difference: bare THROW in a CATCH block re-raises the exact original error with its original number, severity, message, and line — RAISERROR cannot replicate this and always creates a new error record.

Advantages:

  • THROW preserves the original error number when re-raising — the calling C# application receives the exact SQL error code for type-specific handling (deadlock vs constraint violation vs custom business error)
  • THROW always terminates the current batch — RAISERROR with severity below 20 allows execution to continue, a common source of incomplete error handling
  • THROW's simpler syntax requires no severity/state/format string parameters — less boilerplate, more readable stored procedures

Fintech Example: A payment procedure originally used RAISERROR to re-raise caught errors, but RAISERROR creates a new error — the C# application always received the same RAISERROR number (50000), unable to distinguish a deadlock from a constraint violation. Switching to bare THROW in the CATCH block preserved the original SQL error numbers, enabling the application to implement deadlock-specific retry (1205) vs user-facing validation messages (2627) vs business rule rejections (50001+).

followUps.question: What is TRY...CATCH in T-SQL?
followUps.answer:
Definition: TRY...CATCH is SQL Server's structured error handling introduced in SQL Server 2005. Runtime errors with severity 11+ inside the TRY block transfer control to the CATCH block. CATCH provides ERROR_MESSAGE(), ERROR_NUMBER(), ERROR_SEVERITY(), ERROR_STATE(), ERROR_LINE(), and ERROR_PROCEDURE() to capture full error context. THROW in CATCH re-raises the original error; SELECT inside CATCH can log it before re-raising.

Advantages:

  • Enables atomic rollback on error — CATCH block checks IF @@TRANCOUNT > 0 ROLLBACK before logging and re-raising, preventing partial transaction commits
  • Centralises error logging to a database audit table within the CATCH block — every failure is captured regardless of which application or user triggered it
  • Mirrors C# try/catch structure, making stored procedure error logic familiar and readable to .NET developers who also maintain database code

Fintech Example: A payment disbursement procedure wraps debit/credit operations in TRY/CATCH. On any error, CATCH rolls back the transaction, inserts into PaymentErrorLog with ERROR_MESSAGE(), ERROR_LINE(), and the payment ID, then THROW re-raises. Operations teams can query PaymentErrorLog for any failed payment to see the exact SQL error that caused it — critical for diagnosing payment failures without application log access.

followUps.question: What does SET XACT_ABORT ON do with THROW?
followUps.answer:
Definition: When SET XACT_ABORT ON is combined with THROW in TRY/CATCH, they create a robust pattern: XACT_ABORT automatically rolls back the transaction on any unhandled runtime error (including errors outside the TRY block), while THROW in CATCH re-raises the original error with full context. Together they guarantee both complete rollback and accurate error propagation to the calling application.

Advantages:

  • XACT_ABORT handles errors that occur before the TRY block can execute (e.g., compile-time errors in dynamic SQL) — closing the gap in error coverage
  • Bare THROW in CATCH preserves the original error number — the C# SqlException.Number is the actual SQL Server error code, not a RAISERROR wrapper
  • The combination is idiomatic SQL Server 2012+ best practice — recommended by Microsoft and most SQL Server books as the standard pattern for transactional stored procedures

Fintech Example: A card authorisation procedure uses SET XACT_ABORT ON and TRY/CATCH with THROW. When a uniqueness violation occurs (duplicate authorisation attempt — error 2627), XACT_ABORT rolls back atomically, the CATCH block logs the duplicate attempt to a FraudAuditLog table, then THROW propagates error 2627 to the C# application which maps it to a "duplicate transaction detected" response — no manual rollback code needed.

followUps.question: What are user-defined error numbers (50001+) in SQL Server?
followUps.answer:
Definition: SQL Server reserves error numbers 1–49999 for system errors. Numbers 50000 and above are available for user-defined errors raised with THROW or RAISERROR. Custom error messages can optionally be registered permanently in sys.messages with sp_addmessage, enabling multilingual message text. Without registration, the message text is provided directly in the THROW statement.

Advantages:

  • Custom error numbers allow the C# application to switch on SqlException.Number for type-specific handling — distinguishing 51001 (insufficient funds) from 51002 (account frozen) without parsing message text
  • Registered messages (sp_addmessage) support multilingual text — SQL Server substitutes the localised message automatically based on client language
  • Creates a formal contract between database and application error handling — stored procedure errors become first-class typed exceptions in the application layer

Fintech Example: A banking application defines: 51001 = Insufficient balance, 51002 = Account frozen, 51003 = Daily transfer limit exceeded. Each stored procedure THROWs the appropriate number. The C# service maps these to typed domain exceptions (InsufficientFundsException, AccountFrozenException) that trigger specific user-facing messages and alerting workflows — no fragile error message string parsing required, and the error contract is documented in a shared constants file.

questions.tip: THROW re-raises the original error cleanly — RAISERROR can't do that. Use THROW in new code.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Table Scan, Index Scan, and Index Seek in SQL Server?
questions.answer:
Definition: A Table Scan reads every row in a heap (table with no clustered index). An Index Scan reads all leaf-level pages of an index sequentially. An Index Seek navigates the B-tree directly to matching rows using the index key — the most efficient operation. SQL Server chooses between them based on estimated selectivity and available indexes. Seek is O(log n); Scan is O(n).

Advantages:

  • Index Seeks reduce I/O from millions of page reads to a handful — converting a scan to a seek is the highest-impact query optimisation
  • SET STATISTICS IO ON reveals logical and physical read counts — high logical reads with a scan signal the need for a better index
  • Understanding when the optimizer legitimately chooses a scan (returning >30% of rows) prevents unnecessary index creation that won't be used

Fintech Example: A fraud screening query WHERE TransactionDate BETWEEN @start AND @end was performing an Index Scan despite an index on TransactionDate. The date range covered 40% of the table — the optimizer correctly chose a scan because seeking and then reading 40% of rows via key lookups would be slower than a sequential scan. Understanding this avoided a misguided attempt to "fix" the scan by adding more indexes.

followUps.question: What causes a Table Scan even when an index exists?
followUps.answer:
Definition: A Table Scan or Index Scan occurs even when an index exists when: a function is applied to the indexed column (YEAR(date), LOWER(name) — makes the column non-sargable), an implicit type conversion exists (INT column compared to VARCHAR parameter), the query returns a large proportion of rows (making a seek+key-lookup chain more expensive than a sequential scan), statistics estimate high row counts, or the index does not cover the query's columns.

Advantages:

  • Identifying non-sargable conditions (functions on indexed columns) and rewriting them restores seeks without adding new indexes
  • Matching parameter data types to column types eliminates implicit conversions that silently disable index seeks
  • Adding INCLUDE columns to existing indexes eliminates key lookups, sometimes converting scans to seeks when the scan was caused by high key lookup cost

Fintech Example: A transaction search WHERE CAST(Amount AS INT) = 100 was scanning the entire Transactions table despite an index on Amount (DECIMAL). CAST on the indexed column prevents the seek. Rewriting to WHERE Amount = 100.00 (matching the column's DECIMAL type) immediately converted the scan to an index seek, reducing logical reads from 48,000 to 8 for this common fraud screening query pattern.

followUps.question: What is a key lookup and when does it happen?
followUps.answer:
Definition: A Key Lookup (also called a Bookmark Lookup) occurs when SQL Server uses a non-clustered index to find matching rows but then needs to go back to the clustered index (base table) to fetch additional columns not included in the non-clustered index. Each key lookup is a separate random I/O operation — expensive at scale when thousands of lookups occur per query execution.

Advantages:

  • Key lookups are visible in the execution plan as a dedicated operator with a cost percentage — identifying them is straightforward
  • Adding the looked-up columns to the non-clustered index's INCLUDE clause eliminates the key lookup — typically the highest-impact index improvement available
  • A single key lookup per query is acceptable; thousands of key lookups per execution (one per matched index row) is a performance problem that grows linearly with result set size

Fintech Example: An account transaction query used a non-clustered index on (AccountId, Status) but needed Amount and Description in the SELECT. The execution plan showed a Key Lookup operator at 85% cost performing 15,000 random I/Os per execution. Adding INCLUDE (Amount, Description) to the index eliminated all key lookups — the query became fully covering, reducing execution time from 3 seconds to 45ms.

followUps.question: How do you read a SQL Server execution plan?
followUps.answer:
Definition: Reading a SQL Server execution plan involves examining physical operators and their costs from right to left, top to bottom (data flows left, operators process right). Key elements to analyse: operator type (Seek vs Scan vs Lookup), cost percentage of each operator, estimated vs actual row count discrepancies, thick arrows indicating large row transfers between operators, and warning symbols indicating missing indexes, implicit conversions, or spills to tempdb.

Advantages:

  • Cost percentage identifies which operator is the bottleneck — focus optimisation effort on the highest-cost operator rather than guessing
  • Estimated vs actual row count discrepancies indicate stale statistics — the optimizer made bad decisions based on incorrect cardinality estimates
  • Missing index hints in the plan provide the exact CREATE INDEX statement SQL Server recommends — a starting point for index tuning

Fintech Example: A settlement report execution plan showed the Sort operator at 78% cost with a thick arrow feeding it — 2 million rows being sorted before aggregation. The sort existed because the GROUP BY column had no index, forcing a sort-based aggregation. Adding an index on the GROUP BY column eliminated the explicit Sort operator, reducing the settlement report from 12 minutes to 90 seconds by replacing the sort with an ordered index scan.

questions.tip: Functions on indexed columns prevent seeks. LIKE with leading wildcard prevents seeks. Check logical reads with SET STATISTICS IO ON.

questions.question: How do you reseed an identity column in SQL Server? What is DBCC CHECKIDENT?
questions.answer:
Definition: DBCC CHECKIDENT is the T-SQL command to check or reset (reseed) the current identity value of a table. DBCC CHECKIDENT ('TableName', NORESEED) reports the current identity value. DBCC CHECKIDENT ('TableName', RESEED, N) sets the next identity value to N+1. After DELETE (which does not reset identity), DBCC CHECKIDENT is used to reset the identity counter manually for test/staging environments.

Advantages:

  • Resets identity counters in staging/test environments after data cleanup via DELETE, preventing IDs from climbing into millions in small test datasets
  • Synchronises identity values after manual SET IDENTITY_INSERT ON inserts that bypass the auto-increment, preventing future PK conflicts
  • DBCC CHECKIDENT with no value syncs the identity to the current maximum row value — safe reseed that avoids PK violations

Fintech Example: A test environment's Transactions table accumulated IDs in the millions after months of daily test runs (DELETE clears data but does not reset identity). Running DBCC CHECKIDENT ('Transactions', RESEED, 0) after each DELETE-based cleanup kept test IDs small and readable — making test logs and debugging outputs manageable rather than referencing transaction IDs like 9,483,271 in a table with 50 test rows.

followUps.question: What is the difference between TRUNCATE and DELETE regarding identity reset?
followUps.answer:
Definition: TRUNCATE TABLE automatically resets the identity column to the table's original seed value (typically 1). DELETE does not reset the identity — rows deleted via DELETE leave the identity counter at its current value. After a large DELETE, the next INSERT uses the next sequential value after the highest previously assigned value, which may be much higher than the current row count.

Advantages:

  • TRUNCATE's automatic identity reset makes it ideal for staging/temporary tables that are cleared and reloaded — IDs always start fresh without manual intervention
  • Understanding the DELETE/identity distinction prevents confusion when test data cleanup via DELETE produces IDs like 50,000 in a table with 10 rows
  • DBCC CHECKIDENT provides manual control over identity reset after DELETE — appropriate when TRUNCATE cannot be used due to FK constraints

Fintech Example: A staging table for payment batch imports uses TRUNCATE before each import cycle — automatic identity reset ensures every import batch starts with ID 1, making batch audit records easy to cross-reference. If DELETE were used instead (required when FK constraints exist on child staging tables), DBCC CHECKIDENT ('StagingPayments', RESEED, 0) must be called explicitly to achieve the same fresh-start identity behaviour.

followUps.question: What is SET IDENTITY_INSERT ON and when do you use it?
followUps.answer:
Definition: SET IDENTITY_INSERT tablename ON allows explicitly inserting specific values into an identity column, bypassing the auto-increment. Only one table per session can have IDENTITY_INSERT ON at a time. It must be explicitly turned OFF after use. Common uses: data migrations where original IDs must be preserved, seeding reference data with known IDs, and restoring deleted rows with their original identity values.

Advantages:

  • Enables data migrations that must preserve original IDs for FK consistency across related tables in the migration
  • Allows seed data scripts to use known, predictable IDs referenced by FK relationships in other seed scripts
  • After manual inserts with SET IDENTITY_INSERT ON, running DBCC CHECKIDENT to sync the counter prevents future PK conflicts from the auto-increment catching up to manually inserted values

Fintech Example: A legacy payment system migration used SET IDENTITY_INSERT Transactions ON to preserve all original TransactionIds — thousands of foreign key references in 12 related tables depended on these IDs. After migration, DBCC CHECKIDENT ('Transactions', RESEED) (with no value) synced the identity counter to the maximum existing ID, ensuring subsequent auto-increment INSERTs do not collide with the migrated values.

followUps.question: Can you have a non-integer identity column?
followUps.answer:
Definition: In SQL Server, identity columns must be of a numeric data type that supports incrementing: tinyint, smallint, int, bigint, decimal(p,0), or numeric(p,0). The most common types are INT and BIGINT. CHAR, NVARCHAR, UNIQUEIDENTIFIER, and other non-numeric types cannot be identity columns. GUIDs as "identity-like" auto-generated values use NEWID() or NEWSEQUENTIALID() as DEFAULT constraints instead.

Advantages:

  • BIGINT identity (2^63 values) is appropriate for high-volume transaction tables that could exhaust INT (2.1 billion) over years of operation
  • DECIMAL(p,0) identity enables custom increment scales — DECIMAL(18,0) provides a very large key space while remaining a numeric identity column
  • NEWSEQUENTIALID() as a default on UNIQUEIDENTIFIER columns provides GUID "identity-like" behaviour with sequential generation, avoiding the fragmentation of NEWID()

Fintech Example: A high-volume payment platform initially used INT IDENTITY for the TransactionId. After projecting 5 billion transactions over 10 years, the team switched to BIGINT IDENTITY before approaching the INT limit of 2.1 billion — a schema migration that required careful coordination across all application layers referencing the TransactionId type. Planning for BIGINT from the start avoids this expensive migration.

questions.tip: TRUNCATE resets identity automatically. DELETE does not — use DBCC CHECKIDENT to reset manually.

questions.question: What are the types of SQL Server backups? Explain Full, Differential, and Transaction Log backups.
questions.answer:
Definition: SQL Server has three backup types that work together. A Full backup is a complete database snapshot — self-contained, restores independently. A Differential backup contains only pages changed since the last Full backup — smaller and faster than another Full. A Transaction Log backup backs up the transaction log since the last log backup — enables point-in-time recovery, works only under Full or Bulk-Logged recovery models.

Advantages:

  • Layered backup strategy (Full + Differential + Log) minimises storage cost while providing point-in-time recovery down to the minute
  • Transaction Log backups also truncate the inactive log portion — preventing transaction log file bloat that can fill disks
  • The ability to restore to a specific minute before an incident (accidental bulk delete, data corruption) is impossible without transaction log backups

Fintech Example: A banking database with Full backups on Sunday, Differential backups nightly, and Transaction Log backups every 15 minutes could recover from an accidental bulk DELETE at 14:47 on Tuesday by restoring: Sunday Full (NORECOVERY) → Monday night Differential (NORECOVERY) → all log backups from Monday night through 14:46 Tuesday (final log WITH RECOVERY). The 15-minute log backup cadence limited data loss to at most 15 minutes.

followUps.question: What is point-in-time recovery and when is it needed?
followUps.answer:
Definition: Point-in-time recovery restores a database to a specific moment — not just to the last full or differential backup, but to any point within the transaction log chain. It requires the Full recovery model and a complete, unbroken chain of transaction log backups from the last restored Full/Differential backup to the target recovery time.

Advantages:

  • Enables recovery from accidental data modifications (bulk DELETE, incorrect UPDATE) by restoring to the exact moment before the mistake
  • Provides the minimum possible recovery point objective (RPO) — data loss is limited to the interval since the last log backup, not since the last full backup
  • Required for financial and regulated systems where data loss beyond minutes is unacceptable under compliance requirements

Fintech Example: A developer accidentally ran DELETE FROM Transactions (no WHERE clause) in production at 15:23. Point-in-time recovery using RESTORE LOG ... WITH STOPAT = '2024-03-15 15:22:59' restored the database to one minute before the accident. All transactions after 15:22 were lost (less than 1 minute of data under the 15-minute log backup schedule) — a vastly better outcome than restoring from the previous night's Full backup and losing a full day of transactions.

followUps.question: What is Copy-Only backup?
followUps.answer:
Definition: A Copy-Only backup is a standalone backup that does not affect the normal backup chain. A regular Full backup resets the differential baseline — subsequent Differential backups only contain changes since that Full. A Copy-Only Full backup bypasses this, allowing a snapshot to be taken (e.g., before a risky deployment) without disrupting the production backup schedule's differential tracking.

Advantages:

  • Enables safe "before deployment" snapshots without breaking the production differential chain — the on-call DBA can restore from the Copy-Only if the deployment fails
  • Allows development teams to get production-like data snapshots for testing without interfering with production backup scheduling
  • Copy-Only Log backups similarly do not break the log chain, allowing log-chain-safe log copies for secondary purposes

Fintech Example: Before each major payment system deployment, the DBA takes a Copy-Only Full backup of the production database. If the deployment causes unexpected data issues, the team can restore from this pre-deployment snapshot without any impact on the production differential backup chain — subsequent nightly Differential backups continue as if the Copy-Only never happened.

followUps.question: What recovery model allows transaction log backups?
followUps.answer:
Definition: Transaction Log backups require the Full or Bulk-Logged recovery model. Under the Simple recovery model, the transaction log is automatically truncated at each checkpoint — log backups are not possible and point-in-time recovery is unavailable. Full recovery model retains the log until explicitly backed up and enables point-in-time recovery. Bulk-Logged recovery minimally logs bulk operations but otherwise behaves like Full.

Advantages:

  • Full recovery model with regular log backups provides the minimum RPO — data loss limited to the log backup interval rather than the full backup interval
  • The log backup also truncates the inactive log portion — preventing transaction log file bloat that would otherwise fill disks under Full recovery
  • Simple recovery model is appropriate for development and staging where point-in-time recovery is not needed — reducing operational overhead

Fintech Example: A bank's production payment database runs under Full recovery with 15-minute log backups — regulatory requirements mandate RPO of less than 30 minutes. The development database uses Simple recovery — no log backups, no log file growth management needed, minimal DBA overhead. Attempting to take a log backup of the development database fails immediately with "The statement BACKUP LOG is not allowed while the recovery model is SIMPLE."

questions.tip: Remember the restore chain: Full → Differential → Log backups. You need all of them in sequence.

questions.question: What are the High Availability solutions in SQL Server? Explain Mirroring, Log Shipping, Replication, and Always On.
questions.answer:
Definition: SQL Server offers several High Availability and Disaster Recovery solutions. Always On Availability Groups (modern, preferred) provide automatic failover with synchronous or asynchronous replicas and readable secondaries. Database Mirroring (deprecated) had one mirror with optional witness. Log Shipping automates log backup and restore to a standby server. Replication distributes data to subscribers for read scale-out, not true HA.

Advantages:

  • Always On AGs provide automatic failover in seconds with zero data loss (synchronous mode) — the highest availability option for financial systems
  • Readable secondary replicas offload reporting queries from the primary, improving OLTP throughput without additional licensing costs
  • Log Shipping is the lowest-cost DR option — no clustering required, manual failover only, but data loss limited to the log backup interval

Fintech Example: A payment processing platform uses Always On AG with synchronous replication to a secondary in the same data centre (zero data loss, automatic failover in <30 seconds for RTO) and asynchronous replication to a third replica in a remote disaster recovery site (near-zero RPO, manual failover for DR scenarios). Readable secondary handles all reporting queries, keeping OLTP insert performance unaffected by reporting load.

followUps.question: What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous availability groups?
followUps.answer:
Definition: Synchronous availability groups commit a transaction on the primary only after the transaction log is hardened to the secondary replica's disk. This guarantees zero data loss on failover. Asynchronous availability groups commit transactions on the primary without waiting for the secondary — lower latency for writes but potential data loss (transactions committed but not yet replicated) if the primary fails before replication catches up.

Advantages:

  • Synchronous mode ensures RPO = 0 — no committed transactions can be lost, critical for financial systems where every transaction must survive failover
  • Asynchronous mode enables geographically distributed DR replicas without the write latency penalty of waiting for cross-region replication to complete
  • Mixed mode (synchronous local secondary + asynchronous remote secondary) provides both local HA (zero data loss) and geographic DR (manageable data loss)

Fintech Example: A UK payment processor uses synchronous AG replication to a secondary in the same London data centre — automatic failover with zero data loss for local failures. A third replica in Dublin uses asynchronous replication for EU DR compliance — slightly behind the primary but failover there is manual and only triggered for regional disasters where sub-second RPO is not achievable anyway.

followUps.question: What is Failover Cluster Instance (FCI) vs Availability Groups?
followUps.answer:
Definition: A Failover Cluster Instance (FCI) protects the SQL Server instance against server hardware failure — the entire SQL Server instance (with its databases) fails over to another node in the Windows cluster. The databases are on shared storage (SAN). Always On Availability Groups (AG) protect individual databases against server failure — each database has its own copy on each replica, requiring no shared storage.

Advantages:

  • AGs require no shared storage — each replica maintains its own independent copy, eliminating the shared SAN as a single point of failure
  • AGs support readable secondaries — FCIs do not, since only one node runs the instance at a time
  • FCIs protect all databases in the instance simultaneously; AGs protect specific databases and can have different failover policies per database

Fintech Example: A bank runs Always On AGs rather than FCI because their disaster recovery requirements include geographic redundancy (cross-data-centre replicas — impossible with FCI's shared storage constraint) and readable secondaries for reporting (FCI provides no secondary read access). The AG's per-database granularity also allows the low-value archive databases to skip replication entirely, reducing replication bandwidth costs.

followUps.question: What is RTO and RPO in disaster recovery?
followUps.answer:
Definition: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is the maximum acceptable time to restore service after a failure — how long the business can tolerate being down. RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time — how far back the business can recover to. Both drive HA/DR architecture decisions: lower RTO requires faster failover automation; lower RPO requires more frequent backups or synchronous replication.

Advantages:

  • Defining RTO and RPO upfront prevents over-engineering (synchronous replication for a system that can tolerate 1 hour RPO) and under-engineering (log shipping for a system requiring zero RPO)
  • Always On synchronous AG achieves RTO of <30 seconds and RPO of 0 — the highest tier for critical financial systems
  • Log Shipping achieves RTO of hours (manual failover) and RPO of the log backup interval (15–30 minutes) at a fraction of the cost

Fintech Example: A payment gateway's SLA requires RTO < 2 minutes and RPO = 0 — no committed transactions can be lost and service must resume within 2 minutes. This mandates Always On AG with synchronous replication and automatic failover. A regulatory reporting database has RTO < 4 hours and RPO < 30 minutes — Log Shipping with 30-minute log intervals is sufficient and costs significantly less to operate.

questions.tip: Always On AGs are the modern answer. Mirroring is deprecated. Log Shipping is cheap but manual failover.

questions.question: What are DCL commands in SQL? Explain GRANT, DENY, and REVOKE.
questions.answer:
