Definition: DCL (Data Control Language) manages database permissions. GRANT assigns specific permissions to users or roles. DENY explicitly blocks permissions, overriding any GRANT from role membership. REVOKE removes a previously granted or denied permission. DENY always wins over GRANT — a user with GRANT SELECT through a role but DENY SELECT directly cannot SELECT regardless of the role.

Advantages:

  • Role-based permission management (GRANT to roles, add users to roles) scales to hundreds of users without per-user permission management overhead
  • DENY provides an override mechanism — useful for blocking specific users from permissions they inherit through role membership
  • Schema-level GRANT (GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA::dbo) grants permissions on all current and future objects in the schema — reduces permission management as new tables are added

Fintech Example: A payment application database creates AppRole (GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, EXECUTE ON SCHEMA::dbo), ReportingRole (GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA::reporting), and DBARole (db_owner). The web application's service account is in AppRole only. A compliance analyst's account is in ReportingRole only with an explicit DENY DELETE on sensitive tables — even if they are later added to a role with DELETE, the DENY prevents deletion of audit records.

followUps.question: What is the difference between REVOKE and DENY?
followUps.answer:
Definition: REVOKE removes a previously granted or denied permission. DENY explicitly blocks a permission and overrides all GRANTs from any source including role membership. The critical difference: REVOKE is neutral (removes the explicit permission entry, the user's effective access then depends on other grants through roles), while DENY actively blocks the permission regardless of any other grants the user receives.

Advantages:

  • DENY provides a hard block — a terminated employee's account can be DENIED all permissions immediately, overriding all existing role grants until the account is disabled
  • REVOKE is appropriate when removing an explicit permission that should now come from role membership instead — leaves the effective permission determined by roles
  • Understanding the distinction prevents accidental over-permissioning after REVOKE — the user may still have the permission through a role if REVOKE was used instead of DENY

Fintech Example: A fraud analyst is temporarily removed from the AML investigation role (REVOKE the role membership). The analyst still has SELECT on Transactions from a broader AnalystRole. To truly block access during an internal investigation, DENY SELECT ON Transactions TO [analyst_user] is needed — DENY overrides all role-based GRANTs, ensuring no access regardless of current or future role assignments during the investigation period.

followUps.question: What are database roles vs server roles in SQL Server?
followUps.answer:
Definition: Database roles are permission containers scoped to a specific database — members inherit the permissions granted to the role within that database. Server roles are permission containers scoped to the entire SQL Server instance — members have instance-level permissions such as creating databases, managing logins, or server configuration. Fixed roles (db_owner, sysadmin) are pre-defined; custom roles can be created for application-specific permission sets.

Advantages:

  • Custom database roles provide precise, application-specific permission groupings — AppRole with exactly the permissions the web application needs, ReportingRole with read-only access
  • Managing role membership rather than individual user permissions scales to hundreds of users — adding a new developer means adding them to the appropriate role, not granting 50 individual permissions
  • Server-level roles (sysadmin, dbcreator) should be granted sparingly — assigning a web application's service account to sysadmin is a critical security misconfiguration in financial systems

Fintech Example: A banking application's service account is a member of PaymentAppRole (custom database role: SELECT, INSERT on Transactions, EXECUTE on payment stored procedures). It is explicitly not a member of db_owner or any server role. A security audit revealing a service account with sysadmin rights is a critical finding — it means a compromised application could drop databases, create logins, and access any database on the instance.

followUps.question: What is the principle of least privilege in database security?
followUps.answer:
Definition: The principle of least privilege (PoLP) states that every user, process, and service account should have only the minimum permissions required to perform its function — nothing more. In database security this means application service accounts with only the specific tables and procedures they need, no db_owner or sysadmin rights, read-only accounts for reporting, and separate credentials for different application tiers.

Advantages:

  • Limits blast radius of a compromised credential — a web application service account can only access the tables it needs, not drop the database or read unrelated sensitive tables
  • Prevents accidental data destruction — a reporting account with only SELECT cannot accidentally run a DELETE or TRUNCATE even if a query contains one
  • Satisfies regulatory requirements (PCI DSS, SOX, GDPR) that mandate access control and permission documentation for financial data

Fintech Example: A payment gateway's database has five service accounts: WebAppUser (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE on Payments, EXECUTE on payment procedures), ReportingUser (SELECT on reporting schema only), BatchProcessorUser (EXECUTE on batch processing procedures only), MonitoringUser (SELECT on sys.dm_exec_requests, sys.dm_os_wait_stats only), and MigrationUser (db_ddladmin, used only during deployments, disabled between releases). Each account has exactly the permissions for its role and nothing more.

questions.tip: DENY always wins over GRANT — even if the user gets GRANT through a role, an explicit DENY blocks them.

questions.question: What is Fill Factor in SQL Server? What is the default value and when do you change it?
questions.answer:
Definition: Fill Factor determines how full SQL Server fills index leaf pages when building or rebuilding an index — expressed as a percentage from 1 to 100. The default is 0, treated as 100% (fully packed pages). A lower Fill Factor (e.g., 80%) leaves free space on each page for future inserts, reducing the frequency of page splits that cause fragmentation and index maintenance overhead.

Advantages:

  • Appropriate Fill Factor reduces page split frequency on tables with frequent mid-range inserts, improving INSERT throughput and slowing fragmentation accumulation
  • 100% Fill Factor is optimal for append-only tables (monotonically increasing PKs) where inserts never land in the middle of the index
  • Fill Factor is enforced at BUILD/REBUILD time — regular scheduled REBUILD maintenance reinstates the setting as pages fill up over time

Fintech Example: An order management table with GUID primary keys had constant page splits at 100% Fill Factor — each GUID INSERT lands in a random position. Setting FILLFACTOR=75 during REBUILD provided sufficient slack to absorb several weeks of inserts before the next REBUILD threshold was reached, reducing the REBUILD frequency from weekly to monthly and improving average INSERT latency during peak order entry periods.

followUps.question: What is the difference between REBUILD and REORGANIZE for indexes?
followUps.answer:
Definition: REBUILD drops and recreates the index from scratch — fully defragmented pages, statistics updated, Fill Factor reapplied. It requires significant I/O and can be offline (blocking) or online (Enterprise Edition, less blocking). REORGANIZE compacts existing index pages in-place — less I/O, always online, does not update statistics, does not reapply Fill Factor. REBUILD is appropriate above 30% fragmentation; REORGANIZE between 10–30%.

Advantages:

  • REORGANIZE is always online and interruptible — appropriate for tables that cannot tolerate maintenance blocking during business hours
  • REBUILD updates statistics simultaneously — REORGANIZE does not, so UPDATE STATISTICS must be run separately if statistics are also stale
  • REBUILD WITH (ONLINE = ON) in Enterprise Edition allows concurrent queries during the rebuild — essential for high-availability payment systems with narrow maintenance windows

Fintech Example: A payment processing database performs nightly index maintenance: REORGANIZE on indexes with 10–30% fragmentation (quick, non-blocking, sufficient for moderate fragmentation) and REBUILD on indexes above 30% (thorough defragmentation and statistics update in one operation). REBUILD WITH (ONLINE = ON) is used for the largest indexes to avoid blocking overnight batch processes running concurrently with the maintenance window.

followUps.question: What is a page split and why is it bad?
followUps.answer:
Definition: A page split occurs when SQL Server needs to insert a row into a fully packed index page. It creates a new page, moves approximately half the rows to the new page, inserts the new row, and updates the page chain pointers. Page splits are expensive — they write two pages instead of one, immediately create external fragmentation, and increase the total page count of the index.

Advantages:

  • A lower Fill Factor provides free space that absorbs new row inserts without splits — reducing splits reduces fragmentation accumulation rate proportionally
  • Sequential insert patterns (INT IDENTITY PK) only ever append to the last page — page splits never occur regardless of Fill Factor, making 100% Fill Factor optimal
  • Monitoring the SQL Server "Page Splits/sec" Performance Monitor counter quantifies the current split rate and validates Fill Factor adjustments

Fintech Example: An OrderBook table showed 50,000 page splits per second at peak trading load — every GUID-keyed INSERT was splitting a full page. The "Page Splits/sec" counter in SQL Server Performance Monitor confirmed the diagnosis. Setting FILLFACTOR=70 on REBUILD reduced page splits to 8,000 per second (INSERT slots into existing free space most of the time) and visibly improved INSERT latency during the peak trading window.

followUps.question: How does Fill Factor relate to index fragmentation?
followUps.answer:
Definition: Fill Factor and index fragmentation have a direct relationship: lower Fill Factor means more free space on pages at rebuild time, which means more inserts can occur before pages fill up and splits begin, which means fragmentation accumulates more slowly. Higher Fill Factor means denser pages at rebuild but splits begin immediately on new inserts, producing rapid fragmentation on write-heavy tables.

Advantages:

  • Tuning Fill Factor to match the table's write pattern minimises both the initial fragmentation rate and the required REBUILD frequency
  • Append-only tables (INT IDENTITY inserts always at the end) never fragment regardless of Fill Factor — 100% provides maximum read density with no fragmentation downside
  • Measuring fragmentation before and after Fill Factor changes (via sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats) validates that the chosen Fill Factor achieves the desired maintenance frequency

Fintech Example: A high-churn payment table at FILLFACTOR=100 reached 50% fragmentation within 48 hours, requiring a REBUILD every other day. Testing FILLFACTOR=80 extended the time to reach 30% fragmentation from 2 days to 12 days — reducing REBUILD frequency from 3x per week to twice per month while maintaining acceptable query performance throughout the extended maintenance interval.

questions.tip: Fill Factor 0 = 100% full. Lower value = more free space = fewer page splits = less fragmentation over time.

questions.question: What are the Recovery Models in SQL Server? Explain Simple, Full, and Bulk-Logged.
questions.answer:
Definition: SQL Server's recovery model controls how the transaction log is managed. Simple recovery auto-truncates the log after each checkpoint — no log backups possible, no point-in-time recovery. Full recovery retains the full log until explicitly backed up via BACKUP LOG — enables point-in-time recovery. Bulk-Logged recovery minimally logs bulk operations during large ETL loads, then switches back to Full for normal operation.

Advantages:

  • Full recovery with regular log backups provides point-in-time recovery — essential for regulated financial databases where data loss beyond minutes is unacceptable
  • Simple recovery for development/test databases eliminates log file growth management — auto-truncation keeps the log file small without DBA intervention
  • Bulk-Logged recovery temporarily reduces log size during massive ETL loads, then restoring Full recovery maintains the log chain for point-in-time recovery after the load

Fintech Example: A bank's production payment database runs Full recovery with 15-minute log backups — regulatory RPO requirement of <30 minutes. A year-end historical data load switches to Bulk-Logged (50x smaller log for the bulk INSERT of 500 million rows), completes in 2 hours instead of 8, then immediately switches back to Full and takes a log backup to restore the log chain — balancing ETL performance against ongoing recovery capability.

followUps.question: What happens to the transaction log if I forget to take log backups under Full Recovery?
followUps.answer:
Definition: Under the Full recovery model, the transaction log grows continuously until a BACKUP LOG command is executed. Log backup truncates the inactive (committed) portion of the log, freeing space for reuse. If BACKUP LOG is never run, the log file grows until it fills the disk, at which point all transactions fail with error "The transaction log for database X is full due to LOG_BACKUP."

Advantages:

  • Regular log backups (every 15–30 minutes) keep the transaction log file size stable — the inactive portion is truncated after each backup
  • A SQL Server Agent job running BACKUP LOG on a schedule is a simple automation that prevents log growth emergencies
  • Monitoring the log_used_percent column in sys.dm_os_performance_counters provides early warning before the log disk fills

Fintech Example: A payment database was switched to Full recovery for point-in-time recovery capability but log backup jobs were not configured immediately. Over a weekend, the 50GB log drive filled completely — all payment inserts failed with "transaction log is full." Emergency remediation required taking the database briefly offline to run BACKUP LOG TO DISK = 'NUL' (discarding the log, breaking the log chain) to free space. Configuring the log backup job immediately after enabling Full recovery would have prevented the entire incident.

followUps.question: Can you switch between recovery models? What are the implications?
followUps.answer:
Definition: Switching recovery models is permitted but has important implications. Switching from Full to Simple discards the log chain — the log is truncated and point-in-time recovery back through the switch point is no longer possible. Switching back from Simple to Full starts a new log chain from that moment, requiring a new Full or Differential backup to anchor the chain before log backups can be taken for recovery purposes.

Advantages:

  • Planned switches (Full → Bulk-Logged for ETL → Full) are safe if a Full backup is taken after switching back to Full, re-anchoring the new log chain
  • Understanding the chain-breaking implications prevents the mistake of switching to Simple for maintenance and then expecting the prior log chain to remain valid
  • Taking a FULL BACKUP immediately after switching from Simple or Bulk-Logged back to Full establishes the new chain anchor required for subsequent log backups

Fintech Example: A payment database performs quarterly maintenance switches: Full → Bulk-Logged (large index REBUILD, massive log savings) → Full (immediately followed by BACKUP DATABASE to anchor the new chain) → log backups resume every 15 minutes. The two weeks of prior log backups before the switch are discarded from the restore chain at the point of the switch, but the new full backup anchors a fresh chain for all future recovery needs.

followUps.question: What is a log chain and why does it matter for restore?
followUps.answer:
Definition: The log chain is an unbroken sequence of transaction log backup files where each log backup begins exactly where the previous one ended. To restore a database to a specific point in time, every log backup in the chain from the last Full/Differential backup to the target time must be present and unbroken. Any gap in the chain (missing log backup, switch to Simple recovery) breaks the chain and prevents point-in-time recovery past that break point.

Advantages:

  • An intact log chain is the prerequisite for point-in-time recovery — monitoring chain integrity is as important as the backups themselves
  • RESTORE HEADERONLY on each log backup file verifies the chain — the FirstLSN of each backup must match the LastLSN of the previous one
  • Storing log backups in a separate location from the Full backup ensures a single storage failure cannot break both the anchor and the chain

Fintech Example: A bank's disaster recovery test revealed that one night's log backup job had silently failed due to a disk permission error — the log chain had a 30-minute gap. Point-in-time recovery to any time after that gap was impossible. The gap was only discovered during DR testing, not in production. Implementing log backup success monitoring (alerting on any failed BACKUP LOG) and weekly DR test restores would have surfaced the gap within hours rather than months.

questions.tip: Under Full Recovery, if you don't take regular log backups, the log file grows forever — set up a SQL Agent job.

questions.question: What are the types of SQL commands? Explain DDL, DML, DQL, DCL, and TCL.
questions.answer:
Definition: SQL commands are classified into five categories: DDL (Data Definition Language — CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME) defines database structure. DML (Data Manipulation Language — INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE) modifies data. DQL (Data Query Language — SELECT) queries data. DCL (Data Control Language — GRANT, DENY, REVOKE) manages permissions. TCL (Transaction Control Language — COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT) manages transactions.

Advantages:

  • Understanding DDL vs DML clarifies which operations can be rolled back (DML — yes, within a transaction; DDL in most databases — auto-committed) and which fire triggers (DML — yes; DDL — only via DDL triggers)
  • TCL commands give explicit control over transaction boundaries — critical for multi-step financial operations requiring atomicity
  • DCL commands implement least-privilege access control — granting the minimum necessary permissions per service account

Fintech Example: A payment system deployment script uses all five categories: DDL (ALTER TABLE Payments ADD ProcessedAt DATETIME2), DML (UPDATE Payments SET ProcessedAt = CreatedAt WHERE ProcessedAt IS NULL), DCL (GRANT SELECT ON Payments TO ReportingRole), TCL (BEGIN TRAN / COMMIT surrounding the DML), and DQL (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Payments to validate the migration result) — each category serving a distinct role in the deployment procedure.

followUps.question: Why is TRUNCATE a DDL command if it removes data?
followUps.answer:
Definition: TRUNCATE is classified as DDL rather than DML because it operates at the storage allocation level rather than the row level. TRUNCATE deallocates entire data pages (a structural/storage operation) rather than deleting individual rows (a data operation). It does not generate individual row deletion records in the transaction log, does not fire DELETE triggers, bypasses row-level constraints checks, and resets the identity counter — all structural behaviours that place it in the DDL category.

Advantages:

  • Understanding TRUNCATE as DDL explains why it is orders of magnitude faster than DELETE — deallocating pages versus logging millions of individual row deletions
  • TRUNCATE's DDL classification explains why it cannot be used when FK references exist — it bypasses the row-level FK checks that DELETE performs
  • Knowing TRUNCATE is DDL-category but transactional in SQL Server (unlike Oracle/MySQL) prevents the misconception that TRUNCATE is never rollback-able

Fintech Example: A staging database pipeline uses TRUNCATE on staging tables between ETL runs — the DDL classification means no triggers fire (no accidental audit log entries for staging data), no individual row deletions are logged (the staging table can be 10 million rows and TRUNCATE completes in milliseconds), and the identity resets automatically. These DDL-category behaviours are exactly why TRUNCATE is the correct choice for staging table resets.

followUps.question: Can you roll back a DDL statement?
followUps.answer:
Definition: In SQL Server, DDL statements (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE) can be rolled back if they are inside an explicit transaction that has not yet been committed. This differs from Oracle and MySQL where DDL statements cause an implicit COMMIT. SQL Server treats all DDL as transactional within explicit transactions, making DDL rollback possible — a significant safety feature for deployment scripts.

Advantages:

  • Wrapping all DDL and DML in a deployment script inside a single transaction with a ROLLBACK at the end enables safe "dry run" testing in production
  • An error during a multi-step DDL deployment can automatically rollback all prior DDL steps via SET XACT_ABORT ON, preventing partially applied schema changes
  • This behaviour is unique to SQL Server — developers from Oracle or MySQL backgrounds must explicitly learn that SQL Server DDL is rollback-able

Fintech Example: A payment schema migration script wraps 12 DDL statements (ALTER TABLE, CREATE INDEX, DROP COLUMN) in BEGIN TRAN / COMMIT with SET XACT_ABORT ON. If any statement fails (e.g., a new NOT NULL column with no DEFAULT on a non-empty table), the entire transaction rolls back automatically — the production database is left in exactly its pre-migration state, preventing partially applied schema changes that could break the running application.

followUps.question: What is the difference between DELETE and TRUNCATE in terms of transaction logging?
followUps.answer:
Definition: DELETE generates individual row deletion records in the transaction log — one log record per deleted row. This enables row-level rollback, fires DELETE triggers, and respects FK constraints with each row checked individually. TRUNCATE generates minimal log records — only page deallocation operations. This makes TRUNCATE orders of magnitude faster for large tables but means individual row deletions are not logged and triggers do not fire.

Advantages:

  • DELETE's full logging enables point-in-time recovery — individual row deletions can be reversed by reading the transaction log
  • TRUNCATE's minimal logging means it completes in milliseconds on 100 million row tables — DELETE would take hours and generate enormous log files
  • Understanding the logging difference explains why compliance systems always use DELETE (full audit trail) while ETL pipelines use TRUNCATE (performance)

Fintech Example: A compliance team investigating a data incident needed to confirm exactly when specific transaction records were deleted and what their values were. Because the production system used DELETE (not TRUNCATE) for all data removals, the DBA was able to read the transaction log using fn_dblog() to confirm the deletion timestamps, the deleted values, and the SQL login that performed the deletion — evidence impossible to reconstruct from a TRUNCATE operation's minimal log records.

questions.tip: DDL auto-commits (can't rollback). DML is transactional (can rollback). TRUNCATE is DDL so it's not rollbackable in most RDBMS.

questions.question: What is a CASE statement in SQL? Explain SIMPLE vs SEARCHED CASE with examples.
questions.answer:
Definition: A CASE statement provides conditional logic in SQL — evaluating conditions and returning different values based on which condition matches first. Simple CASE compares one expression to multiple values (like a switch statement). Searched CASE evaluates independent boolean conditions for each WHEN clause (like if-else chains). CASE can appear in SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, and UPDATE SET clauses.

Advantages:

  • Enables conditional aggregation (COUNT/SUM + CASE) for pivot-style reports — counting or summing different subsets of rows in a single query pass
  • CASE in ORDER BY enables custom sort ordering not expressible with simple column references
  • CASE in UPDATE SET applies different transformations to different rows in a single UPDATE statement without multiple passes or application-layer looping

Fintech Example: A settlement summary report uses CASE-based conditional aggregation: SELECT COUNT(CASE WHEN Status='Settled' THEN 1 END) AS SettledCount, COUNT(CASE WHEN Status='Failed' THEN 1 END) AS FailedCount, SUM(CASE WHEN Status='Settled' THEN Amount ELSE 0 END) AS SettledAmount FROM Transactions GROUP BY MerchantId — computing all four metrics in one query pass rather than four separate queries per merchant.

followUps.question: What is the difference between CASE and IIF() in SQL Server?
followUps.answer:
Definition: IIF() is a SQL Server shorthand for a two-branch CASE expression: IIF(condition, true_value, false_value) is exactly equivalent to CASE WHEN condition THEN true_value ELSE false_value END. IIF() is less portable (SQL Server and Access only) and only handles two outcomes. CASE is ANSI SQL standard, works on all databases, and supports any number of branches with arbitrary conditions.

Advantages:

  • IIF() is more concise for simple boolean conditions with two possible outcomes — readable inline without the CASE/WHEN/THEN/END boilerplate
  • CASE is the correct choice for three or more branches, complex conditions, or code that must be portable to other database systems
  • Both produce identical execution plans — the choice is purely syntactic preference, not a performance consideration

Fintech Example: A transaction risk flag column: IIF(Amount > 10000, 'High', 'Normal') AS RiskFlag is concise for the binary outcome. When the business adds Medium risk (Amount 5000–10000), the IIF must be rewritten to a CASE expression anyway — using CASE from the start: CASE WHEN Amount > 10000 THEN 'High' WHEN Amount > 5000 THEN 'Medium' ELSE 'Normal' END avoids the rewrite when additional risk tiers are added.

followUps.question: Can you use CASE in a WHERE clause?
followUps.answer:
Definition: CASE can be used in a WHERE clause to create conditional filter logic — applying different conditions based on a parameter value or column value. The CASE evaluates to a value that is then compared, enabling dynamic WHERE clause logic without dynamic SQL. This is useful for optional filters where the condition should be ignored when the parameter is NULL.

Advantages:

  • CASE in WHERE enables optional parameter filtering without dynamic SQL or multiple query branches: WHERE StatusId = CASE WHEN @filter IS NULL THEN StatusId ELSE @filter END
  • Avoids the need for IF/ELSE blocks creating multiple nearly-identical query versions for different filter combinations
  • CASE expressions in WHERE are sargable if the evaluated column is indexed — unlike functions on indexed columns

Fintech Example: A transaction search stored procedure has an optional @Status parameter: WHERE TransactionDate BETWEEN @start AND @end AND Status = CASE WHEN @Status IS NULL THEN Status ELSE @Status END. When @Status is NULL, Status = Status is always true (matching all rows). When @Status = 'Pending', it filters to pending only. One query handles both cases without IF/ELSE branching or dynamic SQL.

followUps.question: How do you handle NULLs in CASE expressions?
followUps.answer:
Definition: CASE expressions handle NULL differently from other comparisons. In Simple CASE, WHEN NULL is never matched — NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN in SQL. To match NULL values, use Searched CASE with WHEN column IS NULL. In the ELSE clause, if no WHEN matches (including NULL input in Simple CASE), NULL is returned by default if no ELSE is specified — a common source of unexpected NULL results.

Advantages:

  • Using WHEN column IS NULL in Searched CASE explicitly handles NULL inputs, preventing them from silently falling through to the ELSE clause
  • Always including an ELSE clause prevents unexpected NULLs appearing in output when no WHEN condition matches
  • COALESCE wrapping CASE output — COALESCE(CASE ... END, 'Default') — provides a final NULL safety net for results used in string concatenation or calculations

Fintech Example: A merchant status display query: CASE Status WHEN 'Active' THEN 'Trading' WHEN 'Suspended' THEN 'Suspended' END AS DisplayStatus produced NULL for merchants with Status = NULL (onboarding, not yet active). The NULL appeared as a blank in the UI, confusing the onboarding team. Fixing to CASE WHEN Status IS NULL THEN 'Onboarding' WHEN Status = 'Active' THEN 'Trading' WHEN Status = 'Suspended' THEN 'Suspended' ELSE 'Unknown' END made all states explicit and eliminated NULL display issues.

questions.tip: CASE is evaluated left to right — first matching WHEN wins. NULLs don't match with = in CASE; use WHEN column IS NULL.

questions.question: What is a Self Join in SQL? When and why would you use one?
questions.answer:
Definition: A self-join joins a table to itself using two different aliases, modelling relationships between rows within the same table. The canonical use case is a hierarchical table where each row has a FK pointing to another row in the same table — an Employee table where ManagerId references another EmployeeId. Always use aliases; LEFT JOIN preserves root nodes (e.g., the CEO with no manager).

Advantages:

  • Models employee-manager, category-parent, and account-referral hierarchies in a single table without requiring a separate relationship table
  • Enables row-to-row comparisons — employees earning more than their manager, accounts in the same branch, transactions from the same device
  • Composable with window functions — self-join with a date offset can compare each transaction to the previous one in a running period analysis

Fintech Example: A relationship manager hierarchy table uses a self-join to display each RM alongside their regional director: SELECT rm.Name AS RM, rd.Name AS RegionalDirector FROM RelationshipManagers rm LEFT JOIN RelationshipManagers rd ON rm.ManagerId = rd.RmId. Regional directors with no manager (top of the hierarchy) still appear with NULL as Regional Director — the LEFT JOIN ensures no RM is excluded from the report regardless of hierarchy depth.

followUps.question: How would you model a self-referential relationship in EF Core?
followUps.answer:
Definition: In EF Core, a self-referential relationship is configured with HasOne and HasMany navigation properties pointing to the same entity type. The Employee entity has a Manager navigation property (HasOne, nullable) and a DirectReports collection (HasMany). EF Core generates the self-join SQL automatically when LINQ traverses these navigations — Include(e => e.Manager) or Include(e => e.DirectReports).

Advantages:

  • EF Core generates the self-join SQL automatically — no manual JOIN writing needed when traversing Manager or DirectReports navigations in LINQ
  • Include(e => e.Manager) eagerly loads the manager in one query, preventing N+1 when displaying manager names alongside employee records
  • Configuring the relationship as nullable (HasOne(e => e.Manager).WithMany(e => e.DirectReports).IsRequired(false)) correctly models root nodes with no manager

Fintech Example: A financial advisor CRM models the self-referential hierarchy: modelBuilder.Entity<Advisor>().HasOne(a => a.Manager).WithMany(a => a.DirectReports).HasForeignKey(a => a.ManagerId).IsRequired(false). Loading advisors with their managers: context.Advisors.Include(a => a.Manager).Where(a => a.Region == "EMEA") generates a single LEFT JOIN self-join query — EF Core handles the alias management and ON clause automatically.

followUps.question: What is the difference between a self join and a recursive CTE for hierarchical data?
followUps.answer:
Definition: A self-join handles shallow hierarchies by joining the table to itself a fixed number of times — one JOIN per level. A recursive CTE handles hierarchies of arbitrary depth by referencing itself iteratively until no more rows are returned. Self-joins require knowing the maximum depth at query-design time; recursive CTEs handle any depth dynamically.

Advantages:

  • Recursive CTEs traverse hierarchies of any depth without knowing the level count — a flat 2-level self-join cannot traverse a 10-level org chart
  • Self-joins are simpler and potentially faster for exactly 2 levels (e.g., employee and their immediate manager) — no recursion overhead
  • Recursive CTEs build path strings and level counts naturally during traversal — capabilities not available with static self-joins

Fintech Example: An account ownership hierarchy for AML purposes can be 1 to 15 levels deep (individual → holding company → intermediate holding → parent group). A recursive CTE handles all depths with one query regardless of nesting. A self-join approach would require 15 chained LEFT JOINs that only handle up to 15 levels and produce a very wide result set with a column per level — the recursive CTE is far more maintainable and flexible.

followUps.question: How do you avoid duplicate rows in a self join?
followUps.answer:
Definition: In a self-join that compares pairs of rows (e.g., finding customers in the same city), the join condition a.Id < b.Id (or a.Id != b.Id with a.Id < b.Id) prevents duplicate pairs. Without this condition, the result includes both (A,B) and (B,A) as separate rows, and also each row matched with itself (A,A). The less-than condition ensures each pair appears exactly once and self-matches are excluded.

Advantages:

  • The Id < Id condition halves the result set for pair-finding queries — only the canonical (smaller, larger) pair is returned, not both orderings
  • Prevents self-matches (A joined to A) without requiring a separate NOT IN or anti-join condition
  • The condition is index-friendly — it can still use the primary key index for the join, unlike a DISTINCT approach that requires a sort

Fintech Example: A suspicious transaction pattern detection query finds pairs of accounts conducting circular transactions — money from A to B and B to A within 24 hours: SELECT t1.AccountId AS Sender, t2.AccountId AS Receiver FROM Transactions t1 JOIN Transactions t2 ON t1.ToAccountId = t2.AccountId AND t2.ToAccountId = t1.AccountId AND t1.AccountId < t2.AccountId WHERE ABS(DATEDIFF(HOUR, t1.Timestamp, t2.Timestamp)) < 24. The AccountId < AccountId condition ensures each circular pair is reported once.

questions.tip: Always use aliases in self joins. Use LEFT JOIN to include top-level records (like CEO with no manager). Recursive CTEs are better for deep hierarchies.

questions.question: What is a Cursor in SQL Server? When should you use one and when should you avoid it?
questions.answer:
A cursor is a database object that allows you to process query results row-by-row, like a loop in application code. Think of it as a pointer that moves through a result set one row at a time.

Basic cursor syntax:

DECLARE @EmployeeId INT, @Name NVARCHAR(100), @Salary DECIMAL(10,2);

-- Declare the cursor
DECLARE emp_cursor CURSOR FOR
    SELECT EmployeeId, Name, Salary FROM Employees WHERE Department = 'Sales';

-- Open it (executes the query)
OPEN emp_cursor;

-- Fetch first row
FETCH NEXT FROM emp_cursor INTO @EmployeeId, @Name, @Salary;

-- Loop through rows
WHILE @@FETCH_STATUS = 0
BEGIN
    -- Process each row
    PRINT 'Processing: ' + @Name + ' - Salary: ' + CAST(@Salary AS VARCHAR);
    
    -- Do something with this row...
    
    -- Fetch next row
    FETCH NEXT FROM emp_cursor INTO @EmployeeId, @Name, @Salary;
END;

-- Always clean up
CLOSE emp_cursor;
DEALLOCATE emp_cursor;

When cursors are actually justified:

  • Row-by-row processing that truly can't be set-based (rare)
  • Calling a stored procedure for each row
  • Complex calculations that depend on previous row results
  • Administrative/maintenance tasks that must be logged per-row

⚠️ When to AVOID cursors (almost always):

Cursors are slow because SQL Server is optimized for set-based operations, not row-by-row iteration. A cursor on a million rows might take minutes; the equivalent set-based UPDATE takes seconds.

-- BAD: Cursor to give 10% raise to all Sales employees
DECLARE @Id INT
DECLARE c CURSOR FOR SELECT EmployeeId FROM Employees WHERE Department = 'Sales'
OPEN c
FETCH NEXT FROM c INTO @Id
WHILE @@FETCH_STATUS = 0
BEGIN
    UPDATE Employees SET Salary = Salary * 1.10 WHERE EmployeeId = @Id
    FETCH NEXT FROM c INTO @Id
END
CLOSE c; DEALLOCATE c;

-- GOOD: Set-based — one statement, much faster
UPDATE Employees 
SET Salary = Salary * 1.10 
WHERE Department = 'Sales';

Cursor alternatives I use instead:

  • WHILE loop with MIN() to iterate — slightly faster than cursor
  • Set-based UPDATE/INSERT/MERGE for bulk changes
  • Recursive CTEs for hierarchical processing
  • Application-side processing — pull data to C#, process in memory, write back

My general rule: if I find myself reaching for a cursor, I take 5 minutes to think about a set-based alternative first. 9 out of 10 times, one exists.

followUps.question: What is the difference between STATIC, DYNAMIC, FAST_FORWARD cursor types?
How do you optimize a cursor if you absolutely must use one?
What is a WHILE loop alternative to cursors?

questions.tip: FAST_FORWARD cursors are the fastest type if you must use one — read-only, forward-only. But set-based is almost always better.

questions.question: What is the COALESCE() function in SQL Server? How is it different from ISNULL()?
questions.answer:
Both handle NULL substitution, but they differ in portability, number of arguments, and how SQL Server evaluates them.

COALESCE() — ANSI SQL standard. Returns the first non-NULL expression from a list of any number of arguments. Can accept multiple values.

ISNULL() — SQL Server-specific. Accepts exactly two arguments. Slightly faster in SQL Server due to being a native function.

-- COALESCE: returns first non-NULL value from the list
SELECT COALESCE(NULL, NULL, 'Third', 'Fourth') -- returns 'Third'

-- ISNULL: only two arguments
SELECT ISNULL(NULL, 'Fallback') -- returns 'Fallback'

-- Practical example: show nickname if available, otherwise full name
SELECT 
    COALESCE(NickName, FirstName + ' ' + LastName, 'Unknown') AS DisplayName
FROM Employees;

-- Phone number priority: work > mobile > home
SELECT 
    EmployeeId,
    COALESCE(WorkPhone, MobilePhone, HomePhone, 'No phone') AS ContactNumber
FROM Employees;

-- ISNULL equivalent — only handles single fallback
SELECT ISNULL(WorkPhone, 'No phone') AS ContactNumber FROM Employees;

-- Key difference: data type inference
-- COALESCE returns type based on data type precedence of all args
-- ISNULL returns the data type of the first argument (can truncate!)
DECLARE @x NCHAR(3) = NULL;
SELECT ISNULL(@x, 'Fallback');    -- returns 'Fal' (truncated to NCHAR(3)!)
SELECT COALESCE(@x, 'Fallback'); -- returns 'Fallback' (uses higher precedence type)

-- Common use in SUM with NULLs
SELECT SUM(COALESCE(Discount, 0)) AS TotalDiscount FROM Orders;
-- Same as: SUM(ISNULL(Discount, 0))

-- COALESCE with NULL check in WHERE
SELECT * FROM Products
WHERE COALESCE(DiscontinuedDate, '9999-12-31') > GETDATE();

My rule: Use COALESCE for portability and when you need multiple fallback values. Use ISNULL when performance is critical in SQL Server and you have exactly two values — it's marginally faster. Watch the data type truncation trap with ISNULL.

followUps.question: What is the data type truncation issue with ISNULL?
Can COALESCE cause issues with non-deterministic functions being evaluated multiple times?
How does NULLIF() differ from COALESCE?

questions.tip: COALESCE = ANSI standard, multiple args, returns first non-NULL. ISNULL = SQL Server only, 2 args, slightly faster. Watch: ISNULL uses the first argument's data type (can truncate). Use COALESCE for portability.

questions.question: What is the difference between DBMS and RDBMS?
questions.answer:
A fundamental theory question. The key distinction is that RDBMS enforces relationships between tables using foreign keys and referential integrity — which a basic DBMS doesn't do.

FeatureDBMSRDBMS
Full formDatabase Management SystemRelational DBMS
Data storageFiles, hierarchical, networkTables (rows and columns)
RelationshipsNo enforced relationshipsForeign keys enforce referential integrity
KeysNo concept of primary keyPrimary key, foreign key, unique key
ACIDNot necessarily ACIDFull ACID compliance
NormalizationNot supportedSupported (1NF, 2NF, 3NF)
ExamplesXML DBMS, file systems, IMSSQL Server, MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle
Query languageNo standard query languageSQL (Structured Query Language)
-- RDBMS enforces relationships with foreign keys
CREATE TABLE Customers (
    CustomerId INT PRIMARY KEY,
    Name NVARCHAR(100)
);

CREATE TABLE Orders (
    OrderId INT PRIMARY KEY,
    CustomerId INT NOT NULL,
    OrderDate DATETIME,
    FOREIGN KEY (CustomerId) REFERENCES Customers(CustomerId)
    -- RDBMS prevents inserting an order for non-existent customer
    -- A basic DBMS would not enforce this!
);

-- Referential integrity in action
INSERT INTO Orders VALUES (1, 999, GETDATE()); -- ERROR if CustomerId 999 doesn't exist

In practice, everything we work with as .NET developers — SQL Server, MySQL, PostgreSQL — is an RDBMS. The distinction matters in interviews as a theory question, and it's worth noting that modern NoSQL databases like MongoDB are technically DBMS (not RDBMS) because they don't enforce relational constraints.

followUps.question: Is MongoDB a DBMS or RDBMS?
What are the Codd's 12 rules for RDBMS?
Can you use an RDBMS without normalizing your data?

questions.tip: DBMS = manages data files (no enforced relationships). RDBMS = tables + foreign keys + ACID + SQL. All SQL Server/MySQL/PostgreSQL are RDBMS. NoSQL (MongoDB, Redis) are DBMS variants. The key difference: referential integrity enforcement.
